title: Qld child safety minister axes key survey of children in care
text:
Queensland's child safety minister said she "had no hesitation" in axing a key survey, that she previously lauded as integral.

The My Life in Care Survey has been conducted every year since 2022, but minister Amanda Camm today confirmed it had been quashed.

This despite her once labelling the survey as a "cornerstone" of the Government's approach to tackling the broken child safety system, and proof that it was "on the right track".

The outcomes of the 2024 survey were tabled as part of a submission to the now-finalised Child Safety Inquiry.

Ms Camm's comments were in a draft foreword as part of that submission.

The outcomes of the 2024 survey were tabled as part of a submission to the now-finalised Child Safety Inquiry. (ABC News: Daryna Zadvirna)

"We will use what we learn from the My Life in Care survey each year to check on our progress, assess the impact of our reforms and continually refine our approach," Ms Camm said.

The survey asks teens and children a number of questions, including their background, how they felt coming into care versus how they felt now, whether they felt that had sufficient privacy, safety and security and felt cared for.

In 2024, nearly 1,000 youths between the ages of 10 and 18 responded to the survey, and 88 children aged between five and nine responded.

It stated in that year, 40 per cent of children aged between 10 and 18 had made a complaint about their time in care, of those, 39 per cent were unhappy with how their report was handled.

But Ms Camm said the survey wasn't an accurate representation of the experiences of children in care, pointing out the survey stated 67 per cent felt happy in care.

"The Children in Care census outlined the real facts of children in care and the fact that over 69% of children coming into care had suffered more than three types of abuse," she said.

"This survey painted a picture of a child safety system, one that was full of happy emojis," she said.

She then showed the front of the 2024 survey which contained emojis.

Amanda Camm showed the 2024 report. (ABC News)

Ms Camm also said that children, under the former Labor government had been "bribed" to complete the survey.

Previously, children were given vouchers to grocery stores if they completed the survey.

The Opposition said it was in line with advice from the Queensland Family and Child Commission, stating the views of young people "should be compensated accordingly" through "gift cards, travel subsidies, formal recognition of participation and in-kind renumeration, such as skills building".

Child safety worker union alarmed by possible removal of key reporting tool The union representing child safety workers in Queensland has highlighted concerns about the possible removal of a key reporting tool.

But Ms Camm said it was "unacceptable".

"I will not be guided by a survey that was conducted where children were bribed to answer the survey and given money to answer the survey," Ms Camm said.

"So, I make no apology for axing that."

The removal of the My Life in Care survey removes a complaint mechanism for children in care, despite the state's peak child safety oversight body calling for more to be put in place.

The Queensland Family and Child Commission's Too Little, Too Late report outlines the state's "narrow focus" on the complaints process; reporting that children "fear speaking up about their workers and providers, and [hold] cynicism that their worries would be acted on".

title: Cunningham's anti-trans comments open WNBA to its latest hijacking
text:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

title: Do your kids love blind boxes? There's a potentially darker side
text:
If you're a parent, you're probably familiar with the concept of blind boxes, whether it's Labubus, Pokémon cards or Ooshies.

Blind boxes are products — usually toys — in sealed packaging. The exact item remains a mystery until opened after purchase. Some collections contain "rare" items.

Born in the 80s, my version was Kinder Surprises and Hasbro's L'il Babies.

The concept has exploded in recent years, explains Anastasia Hronis, a clinical psychologist and lecturer at University of Technology Sydney.

"With social media, we have seen blind boxes take off around the world, and a huge surge in popularity.

"These blind box purchases also typically cost more than a Kinder Surprise."

Labubus, for example, cost anywhere from about $30 to thousands of dollars.

While blind boxes can be fun, Dr Hronis says parents should be aware of their similarities with gambling, and understand how to help children make healthy choices around them.

How blind boxes echo gambling

Blind boxes aren't classified as gambling under most legal definitions, but Dr Hronis says they resemble gambling because the buyer pays for an uncertain outcome.

"The thrill comes from the chance of getting a rare, or even sometimes 'secret' item."

She says their design uses "variable-ratio reinforcement".

" This is same reward pattern seen in poker machines, where unpredictable wins keep people coming back. "

César Albarrán-Torres is an associate professor at Swinburne University of Technology.

His research found blind boxes trigger the same emotional states — anticipation, randomness, occasional joy and frequent disappointment — as pokies.

He explains these are the dynamics of gamble play, and there are preliminary indications that using gamble play devices such as claw machines as a child can lead to problems with gambling in adulthood.

Dr Hronis says blind boxes are not "automatically designed to be addictive", but they are designed to be reinforcing, "and to keep people coming back and buying more".

If they're like gambling, shouldn't they be regulated?

Experts say blind boxes trigger the same emotional states as pokies. (Adobe Stock)

Moderating how much children engage with blind boxes can be tricky, Dr Albarrán-Torres says, because their availability is so widespread.

"My colleague and I did a walk-through of Melbourne Central [shopping centre] and found blind boxes everywhere.

"There are anchor shops … but also vending machines in public spaces and official and unofficial products in retail stores and even beauty salons."

Many blind boxes are also connected to things that children love, such as Disney, which Dr Albarrán-Torres says only increases their appeal.

Globally, he says blind boxes are projected to reach annual profits of US$24.2 billion (about A$34 billion) by 2033.

Why it's OK if your child won't wear warm clothing While it can be frustrating for parents and caregivers at times, experts say kids' innate urge to explore independence — like choosing their own clothes — is healthy.

Since 2023, China has prohibited the sale of blind boxes to children under 8. And Singapore is taking steps to regulate them.

"Singapore is the first jurisdiction in the Asia Pacific region where they are trying to enforce regulation for blind boxes," says Dr Albarrán-Torres.

He believes the same should happen here in Australia.

Some manufacturers list the odds of winning and age guidelines in small print on blind boxes.

For example, a label suggesting the product is not for children under 12.

But Dr Albarrán-Torres says these labelling practices are inconsistent, unclear and unregulated.

"It should be regulated better. There should be more consistent approach to how winning probability and age recommendations are displayed.

" We don't want to be the fun police, but there needs to be guard rails. "

Helping kids engage positively with blind boxes

There can be positives to engaging with blind boxes, says Dr Hronis, such as getting children involved with collecting.

"It helps them build patience, and perhaps even helps them with budgeting, similar to other collectable hobbies."

But those benefits depend on the activity "staying bounded and not becoming a repeated chase for a rare outcome," she says.

To help, Dr Hronis suggests:

Discuss setting limits with your child around budget and frequency of purchases. For example, a portion of their pocket money can go towards saving for them.

Avoid using blind boxes as emotional rewards or comfort purchases.

Encourage your child to wait until they get home to open their blind box. Dr Hronis says this avoids a situation of temptation, where a child may open it as soon as they have bought it, and feel tempted to go back in the store and buy another if it isn't what they were hoping for.

Use disappointment as a teaching moment. She says sitting in that feeling together helps kids practise tolerating disappointment without immediately chasing the next thing.

Dr Hronis recommends monitoring your child's blind box use. If it shifts from an occasional treat to a constant preoccupation, it might be time to "press pause" or redirect their interests towards other creative interests or sports.

Dr Albarrán-Torres says not all blind boxes are created equal. Something like footy or Pokémon cards can build skills with card playing, trading and "there is an element of knowledge and community building".

He recommends parents use blind boxes as an opportunity to talk about the issue or risk and chance, and what you're going to lose.

"It's important for parents to have these conversations early."

title: Fatal fires in Sydney and NSW South Coast prompt renewed smoke alarm warning
text:
Two elderly people have died in separate house fires overnight in Sydney and on the New South Wales South Coast.

The blazes at Villawood in Western Sydney and Greenwell Point, east of Nowra, both started within hours of each other last night.

Thirteen people have now died in structure fires across the state this winter.

Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said the two deaths would be felt by firefighters across the state.

"We really feel the impact of these tragedies; it's something our firefighters experience firsthand," he said.

"We extend our condolences to those families, because we have a good understanding of the heartache that they're experiencing."

Cooking fire starts fatal blaze

At 6pm firefighters were called to a house fire at Tuncoee Road in Villawood.

Crews managed to rescue a woman aged in her 50s.

A second woman aged in her 70s died a short time later at Liverpool Hospital while receiving treatment for smoke inhalation.

Jeremy Fewtrell says there has been a concerning rise in fire fatalities this winter. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Mr Fewtrell said investigators worked through the night to determine the cause of the blaze.

"We believe that fire was related to a cooking fire," he said.

"Our fire investigators inspected the property and did not locate a working smoke alarm in the property.

" This really underscores the importance of having a working smoke alarm. "

A separate blaze started inside a mobile home at a tourist park in Greenwell Point, east of Nowra, about 10pm.

After extinguishing the flames, firefighters found the body of an elderly man inside.

Another man was taken to hospital in a serious condition with serious burns and smoke inhalation.

The operations officer for Shoalhaven Rural Fire Service, Anthony Ciccaldo, said crews faced dynamic risks at the scene, including gas bottles and neighbouring mobile homes just metres away.

"Crews were quickly able to get on top of it as soon as they arrived, and knock [the fire] down to reduce any further extension to neighbouring properties," he said.

Rise in fatal winter fires

The deaths mark a sharp rise in fatal fires across the state this year.

During winter last year, there were more than 1,000 house fires resulting in nine fatalities.

This season, 13 people have died as 856 house fires have been recorded across NSW during the colder months.

Mr Fewtrell said while there have been fewer fires this winter, the rise in fatalities was concerning.

"Very sadly this year we're now seeing a significant increase in the number of fire deaths," he said.

"The fundamental aspects of having working smoke alarms are more critical than ever."

The commissioner said elderly people were often over-represented in fire fatality data, due to mobility issues that made escaping a house fire difficult.

"We know that fire safety for elder residents is a really important thing," he said.

"[Residents can] ring the fire station and ask for a safety visit for their parents or their grandparents or their elderly neighbours.

"We'll talk to the residents about fire safety and be able to provide very customised and specific advice for their individual circumstances ... and install smoke alarms free of charge."

title: NSW government reveals blueprint to fit an extra 1.3m people into Sydney
text:
The eastern suburbs will be home to most of Greater Sydney's new housing over the next 20 years, under a New South Wales government blueprint to rebalance the region's growth.

Meanwhile, Western Sydney will drive economic growth, leveraging investment in the area's second airport, the Moorebank Intermodal Precinct and vast industrial lands.

These are the broad strokes of the government's Sydney Plan, which charters how Greater Sydney will find homes and places of work for an extra 1.3 million people by 2046.

Planning Minister Paul Scully described the 20-year vision as a rebalancing of Greater Sydney, with a focus on building upwards rather than outwards by developing green fields.

"We're treating the city as one, even though we recognise there are differences across the expanse of it," he said.

"There'll still be housing in the west, there'll still be jobs growth in the east.

"This is the continuation of the rebalancing of housing growth in Sydney, around where there's existing infrastructure capacity."

Mr Waterford says the plans are welcome.

The Sydney Plan was met with praise by the Committee for Sydney, an urban policy think tank.

"The reality is for too long, we've not made it feasible to have kids and live in an apartment," chief executive Eamon Waterford said.

"We've forced people out further when what they really are looking for is amenity and proximity that they can get with family friendly apartments.

"So this change is a really welcome one."

One effort to avoid a repeat of the current housing crisis is the requirement for councils to have land available and zoned to meet a 30-year housing target, allowing the supply of new builds to quickly be topped up, as these time intensive planning processes would have already been completed.

"Over the next 20 years, Sydney will need at least 800,000 more homes, around 950,000 jobs," Mr Scully said.

"And that's why we're introducing [this] requirement … so that we don't get into the housing situation that we're trying to get ourselves out of today."

Local Government New South Wales said the long-term planning requirement was a "good idea".

"We know that the housing supply crisis in Sydney is so deep that we're not going to be able to dig ourselves out of it in one year or even in five years," President Darcy Byrne, who is also the mayor of Inner West Council, said.

"So a long-term plan for ensuring that there is adequate housing supply is probably something that Sydney should have had a long time ago.

"In the inner west, that's exactly what we're seeking to do, to develop a pipeline of housing supply so that over time this problem can be addressed."

Harmony between the city's east and west?

Not only will eastern Sydney take on the majority of housing growth under the plan, but the variety of housing will be more diverse, including developments like townhouses and apartments.

The justification provided in the report is that the existing investment and infrastructure in the areas can support more people.

"When the Minns government first came to office, there was less housing diversity in Sydney than what there was a century ago," Mr Scully told the ABC.

"That's led to some of the problems that we have today with our housing challenges and our housing prices.

"We need to make sure that our housing mix is as diverse as our population mix."

Mr Scully says the city needs a diverse housing mix. (Four Corners)

Eastern Sydney council areas have already been set high five-year housing targets under the National Housing Accord, accounting for just under half of all new builds.

In comparison, Western Sydney council areas have a target of less than a quarter.

Rather, the focus for the city's west is to leverage its industrial land and assets to "cement its role as a nationally significant economic powerhouse", the plan said.

The area will drive the state's freight, logistics and industrial expansion over the next two decades, making use of Western Sydney International Airport, the Moorebank Intermodal Precinct and extensive industrial land.

Half of Greater Sydney's industrial land will be in the city's west, with 80 per cent of undeveloped industrial land located there.

These factors will be a driving force in job growth, with the government forecasting a 59 per cent rise from 475,000 to 755,000 over the next two decades.

The suburbs that will grow to next level

The plan includes liberalising planning controls and streamlining the planning process with CBDs in Sydney, Parramatta and Bradfield. (Supplied: NSW Government)

Sydney, Parramatta and Bradfield City will still be the main three CBDs across Greater Sydney.

But surrounding them will be a network of dozens of "interconnected centres", hosting jobs, services and economic activity.

These areas include Brookvale, Hornsby, Castle Hill, Marsden Park, St Marys, Rhodes, Burwood, Bondi Junction, Hurstville, Miranda and Narrellan, to name a few.

"There will be a boost to residential growth in those centres in addition to jobs growth, creating more vibrant areas and greater mixed use outcomes," Mr Scully said.

Rouse Hill and Kogarah are identified as "emerging major centres", while Leppington, Five Dock, Edgecliff, Fairfield, Oran Park and Wilton are forecast to be "emerging activity centres".

title: Councils look for guidance from state on data centre applications
text:
A move by a councillor in Perth's northern suburbs to ban data centres has failed, but planners and local government leaders say it highlights the need for clearer guidelines on the rapidly expanding sector.

Suzanne Migdale, a councillor in the City of Stirling, moved a notice of motion on Tuesday night, proposing the council investigate designating data centres as an X-use, making them ineligible for approval in any part of the city.

Ms Migdale told Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth she had many concerns about the centres.

"Research has linked large data centres to community concerns around air quality, noise, water stress and broader public health impacts," she said.

" Many data centres use large volumes of water for cooling. The cooling systems, the fans and backup diesel generators can create noise, and backup generators also contribute to air pollution. "

The motion failed by four votes to eight. Currently there are no applications to build data centres in Stirling.

Data centres 'not defined' in planning codes

Belinda Moharich, a planning lawyer and town planner, said one of the challenges councils faced when asked to decide on planning applications for data centres was that they were not a defined use of land in any planning scheme in Western Australia.

"When a land use is not identified in a planning scheme, then there's a requirement to go through a process of determining, in the first instance, whether you can shoehorn it into some other category — they're being classified as being a warehouse or an industrial land use," Ms Moharich said.

"If there is no best fit then it's considered to be a use not listed, which means that it is potentially capable of approval in any zone within a local planning scheme.

" I think there is a need for some more certainty in approach and I don't think blanket bans are the answer. "

A data centre in Canberra surrounded by houses and apartments. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She said data centres could vary greatly in size and impact, from smaller centres inside city buildings to vast campuses that covered hectares of land, and it would be useful for the state government to issue regulations on how to assess planning applications for data centres.

"I think some guidance will be super helpful because it really puts local governments on the front line of having to manage an emerging land use without the proper tools to do so," she said.

Outer suburbs under pressure

Terresa Lynes is the mayor of Gosnells, in Perth's east, and also the chair of the National Growth Areas Alliance, a peak body for local governments in outer metropolitan areas.

She told Mark Gibson on 102.5 ABC Perth her council approved a data centre last year in the suburb of Maddington.

"It's a $415 million project, which will be eventually a 200-megawatt data centre, which is in the Maddington Industrial area," Ms Lynes said.

"This has caused a bit of angst in the community. It was approved in September last year, when we weren't really seeing that angst from communities around data centres, but then all of the information has come through from the American data centres, which has kind of given people some anxiety."

Gosnells Mayor Terresa Lynes says it's better for communities to set policy around data centres than to try to ban them altogether. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Gosnells council has since developed a policy addressing environmental requirements for data centres, including around water usage and noise.

"If you've got to have a data centre in an area, you want the right sort, the ones that have got the closed loop water system, which means that it's not continually using water," Ms Lynes said.

"The ones that are encasing their backup generators in concrete, and the ones that are using the right sort of filtration system to dispel the heat that is coming off the facility."

More data centre inevitable

Like Belinda Moharich, Ms Lynes said she would like to see leadership from the state government around data centre regulation.

"Currently we don't have any legislation to say they're a data centre. We have to assess them as being a warehouse, not as a data centre.

"You couldn't really ban data centres if there's no legislation for it yet."

She said more data centres were inevitable and it would be preferable for councils to have a say in shaping where they went than trying to stop them outright.

"We've got an opportunity to plan them right, to put them in the right spot. We are not going to be able to not have data centres.

"What we also know is that it's more efficient to have that data stored in one space than spread across multiple buildings."

title: Sexual favours scandal rocks South Korea football association
text:
The Korean Football Association (KFA), the governing body of soccer in South Korea, has issued a public apology for "various controversies", including an allegation that payments were made for sexual favours for foreign referees.

South Korean broadcaster JTBC reported last Thursday, local time, that the KFA had provided such services to foreign referees on multiple occasions in 2011 and 2012, including when the referees were in the country for qualifying matches for the 2014 World Cup and the 2012 London Olympics.

In its news report, JTBC cited a 2016 sports ministry investigation that found the KFA had provided inappropriate entertainment to foreign referees on seven occasions between March 2011 and March 2012, including trips to massage parlours where the fees included the costs of sexual services.

South Korea qualified for the 2012 Olympic Games and the 2014 World Cup.

On social media, the KFA issued a public apology for several controversies, including the team's poor results at this year's World Cup and "media reports regarding events from over a decade ago that even many of our own staff members were unaware of".

"However, we wish to clearly state that such inappropriate conduct or misuse of corporate cards is absolutely not occurring at the association at present," the KFA said, as reported by BBC.

"Our association, which ought to bring joy and exhilaration to football fans through the fierce pursuit of goals and the fair sportsmanship that emerges in the process, has recently lost sight of its fundamental purpose and finds itself in a truly dire situation."

The allegations add to scrutiny of the association over a separate issue involving the appointment of former national team coach Hong Myung-bo.

Hong Myung-bo resigned after the 2026 FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Chung Sung-Jun)

Hong and KFA president Chung Mong-gyu both resigned following the World Cup.

Seoul police raided the KFA's offices on Thursday as part of an investigation related to Hong's appointment, police told Reuters.

Hong returned as national team coach in 2024 after a previous spell in charge from 2013 to 2014. His appointment drew scrutiny after the KFA abandoned a months-long search involving foreign candidates and selected Hong following a brief meeting.

The controversy resurfaced after South Korea's disappointing World Cup campaign ended in a group-stage exit.

Reuters/ABC

title: Trading platforms offer cash vouchers for 'high-risk' investments, watchdog says
text:
Retail investors are allegedly being offered cash vouchers and airline reward points as encouragement to use online platforms for their financial trade, a corporate watchdog has found.

Nine online trading platforms were reviewed by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), including Moomoo, Sharesies and Webull.

Platforms reviewed by ASIC: Interactive Brokers Australia Pty Ltd

Moomoo Securities Australia Ltd

Sharesies Australia Limited

Stakeshop AFSL Pty Ltd

tastytrade Australia Pty Ltd

Tiger Brokers (AU) Pty Limited

Totality Wealth Limited

Trading 212 AU Pty Ltd, and

Webull Securities (Australia) Pty Ltd

Their review found some providers were offering fee-free or discounted trading and other incentives to engage in "high-risk" investments.

ASIC did not attribute individual findings to any one company and said not every company had committed every infraction.

ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said trading platforms were increasingly offering complex financial instruments to users who did not fully understand them.

"These are products where it can be hard to understand, but unfortunately easy to lose money, and easy to lose [it] quickly," she said.

"Take a short-dated exchange trading option. You can put a little bit of money in there, a small amount of money in a small window of time.

" Yes, you can potentially make a lot, but you can really lose a lot. "

"These are not just high complexity, but of course high-risk products."

Practices improved since review

In some entities, the review found:

Deficiencies in target market determinations, including insufficient details on how products met the likely objectives, situations and needs of clients.

in target market determinations, including insufficient details on how products met the likely objectives, situations and needs of clients. Onboarding shortcomings , including limited tailoring of questions and repeated/unlimited attempts to pass onboarding questionnaires.

, including limited tailoring of questions and repeated/unlimited attempts to pass onboarding questionnaires. Unclear client disclosure which failed to explain the risks and costs associated with fractional trading.

Since the review, two of the companies have stopped onboarding new clients while remediation is underway, and five more have improved compliance practices.

One has exited the Australian market entirely.

ASIC said it was considering further regulatory and enforcement action in relation to matters identified in the review.

Monash University's Tamara Wilkinson, who specialises in corporate law and regulation, said the watchdog could crack down on companies by tightening rules.

And it could also look to retail investors to prove their competency before investing, which is done in the United Kingdom.

"What it seems like is happening here with these risky financial products is that there is a bit of a gap in the regulation and the protection of retail investors," Dr Wilkinson said.

"Increasing the regulatory protections in this area would bring it more in line with the rest of Australia's regulatory regime."

Ms Constant urged investors to be hypercritical of the agreements they entered into.

"Don't invest simply because it's easy to invest and access, or because there's an inducement to invest in airline points," she said

"Invest because it's a good investment that you understand, and you know it to be a good investment because you understand it."

title: Ancestral lines united in Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title determination
text:
The Eastern Kuku Yalanji people are celebrating a historic native title determination recognising their rights over more than 200,000 hectares of land on Cape York Peninsula.

The Federal Court sat under a marquee in the Aboriginal community of Wujal Wujal, about 200 kilometres north of Cairns, for Wednesday's consent determination hearing, which was attended by more than 600 traditional owners.

Frances Walker says the court determination in Wujal Wujal is a proud day for the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people. (Supplied: Gregg Maxwell, Cape York Land Council and Maxwell Media)

Local elder Frances Walker said it was a proud day for her people, who were able to unite families from more than 100 ancestral lines to form the largest native title group on Cape York.

"To see the Federal Court on Yalanji Land, we proved to the system that we are the rightful people of this land," she said.

"Our people's strength has always been togetherness … our motto is to stand together and be strong for people and land."

A native title determination is a colourful day of celebration for the traditional owners. (Supplied: Gregg Maxwell, Cape York Land Council and Maxwell Media)

Chief Justice Debra Mortimer said it was a privilege to be on country to "recognise a legal tradition that has existed for thousands of years".

"Despite the terrible history of colonisation, Eastern Kuku Yalanji culture is strong, it's here to stay, your lore is here to stay," she said.

Cape Tribulation is part of the native title determination. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

The determination takes in 217,884 hectares of country along south-eastern Cape York Peninsula, extending from the Annan River in the north to the Daintree River in the south, east of the Great Dividing Range.

This includes prominent landmarks such as Cape Tribulation in the Daintree, Black Mountain near Cooktown, and parts of the Annan, Bloomfield, Daintree, East Normanby, West Normanby and Granite Normanby river systems.

The Jabalbina Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation will be the prescribed body corporate managing and protecting the native title rights.

The gathering had waited years for the Federal Court determination. (Supplied: Gregg Maxwell, Cape York Land Council and Maxwell Media)

Jabalbina's chief operating officer, Kallum Clarke, said that included exclusive native title over about 35 per cent of the determination area, which may affect future access to those areas.

"It's just going to have to go back to getting permission," he said.

"We're recognised as the owners now and it will have to go back to whether Eastern Kuku Yalanji people approve of activities happening."

Mr Clarke said the determination empowered his people to secure funding to manage their country and provide opportunities for the younger generation.

"It just gives my people the opportunity to really tie themselves back to country and simply 'Bunday' — sit on country and just enjoy it without having to worry about any legalities around it because the legalities have been sorted and it's been recognised as ours," he said.

Black Mountain in Kalkajaka National Park, south of Cooktown, is included in the determination. (ABC Far North: Sharnie Kim)

Realisation of decades-long fight

The Eastern Kuku Yalanji people lodged their first native title claim through the Cape York Land Council in December 1994, soon after the Mabo decision created a legal pathway for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to seek recognition of native title.

Elder Kathleen Walker, from Wujal Wujal, said the determination was for everyone in the community: those who began the fight and those who will follow.

"I remember the people before me and the people who come after me," Ms Walker said.

"This is for everyone and so that our stories are never forgotten."

In her closing remarks, Chief Justice Mortimer thanked the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people for their patience with Australia's legal system.

"It is a slow and complicated system and I am sorry that it takes so long," she said.

"I know you will be thinking of all the elders who are not here to see this day."

Hundreds gathered at the Federal Court determination in Wujal Wujal. (Supplied: Gregg Maxwell, Cape York Land Council and Maxwell Media)

Wednesday's determination is the 33rd under the Cape York United #1 Native Title Claim lodged in 2014, which is one of Australia's largest native title claims and seeks to resolve land rights across Cape York Peninsula.

On Friday, the Federal Court will recognise the native title rights of Western Yalanji traditional owners in a separate determination within the United #1 claim.

With additional reporting by Chris Calcino, Jeremy Jones, and Conor Byrne.

title: Mental health experts anticipate another rise in reports in census
text:
Experts are expecting to see a rise in the number of mental health conditions across the country in the census, which they hope will provide a fuller picture of community wellbeing.

Tuesday night's census was just the second time Australians have been asked to report long-term health issues.

It will give the nation's statisticians a comparative piece of data to see the shift in population health since the 2021 census, when about one in 11 Australians reported having a long-term mental health condition, ahead of arthritis and asthma.

At that time, mental health conditions were highest in the Australian Capital Territory and South Australia, where about one in 10 people lived with such conditions, which can include depression and anxiety.

"It provides really important information at an Australian population level for the prevalence of these conditions, and obviously tracking whether things have changed over time," biostatistician Tim Slade said of the data.

Professor Slade, from the University of Sydney's Matilda Centre for Research in Mental Health and Substance Use, expected the latest census to reflect a rise in mental health reports, with recent non-census research showing these conditions remain persistent challenges in the community.

The census again asked Australians to report long-term health conditions, which have lasted more than six months. (Supplied: Australian Bureau of Statistics)

In July, Professor Slade's group published data showing more than one in three young Australians aged 16 to 24 reported mental health conditions by 2022.

"But we have seen an increase in the general population, the whole adult population, in mental health problems," he said.

He said the data produced by Tuesday's census would be valuable to researchers.

"I'm very interested in seeing these results," he said.

A chance to compare amid new challenges

The 2021 census took place amid COVID-19 restrictions and lockdowns, but mental health was already a rising concern before the pandemic.

"In terms of mental health challenges … we were seeing a rise in mental health problems long before the COVID pandemic," Professor Slade said.

"COVID has had an impact on the mental health of the population and particularly among some subgroups of the population."

This week's national survey happened amid similar challenging social conditions, but instead of lockdowns and social distancing, hip-pocket issues such as housing affordability and the cost of living are occupying the minds of many.

Mental health service provider Beyond Blue chief executive Georgie Harman said there had been a rise in demand for services across Australia.

"We know from our own data that psychological distress relating to financial pressure has been increasing over the past four years, which is an important signal given that money worries and mental health conditions can influence each other," she said.

"We're also seeing increased demand for immediate support through our services, and indications that anxiety and depression symptoms may be getting more severe.

"The good news is that we can get onto these issues as soon as they start to emerge and take actions that prevent them from snowballing."

Georgie Harman says the years since the last census have not been without various pressures. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Regions could benefit from mental health data

Census data helps government and non-government groups decide where to distribute resources.

"The census data is another useful source of information that helps many organisations make sense of what's happening and plan for the future so that the whole community benefits," Ms Harman said.

Those living outside major cities, including Steph Schmidt, a psychologist and farmer who lives in South Australia's Mid North, are hoping for more investment in mental health support in the regions.

"From what I've seen on the ground, I wouldn't necessarily think that [the prevalence of mental health conditions] is going to have gone down a whole lot in the last couple of years," she said.

"It's an ongoing issue, whether you are rural, whether you are urban."

Steph Schmidt hopes the data of this year's census can help inform regional mental health support. (Supplied)

Ms Schmidt said while awareness of mental health conditions had increased in recent years, the resources available to communities remained limited.

She said that could extend to diagnosis, and if people were not able to receive clinical assistance for their mental health concerns, they may not be aware of conditions they live with.

That could mean a gap in census data among regional Australians.

"It's only capturing those that are diagnosed as well, so it is tricky," Ms Schmidt said.

"On the other hand, it's also helpful to, I guess, discriminate almost between getting the diagnosis and self-diagnosis."

Ms Schmidt said closing the gap between urban and regional spending on services was important, and results from the census may help bridge the divide.

"Things like the census and the responses that come through I hope do help inform where some of that money goes and the services that are supported," she said.

"I think that's where it is really important to answer honestly with where your experience has been so that it can help government, or also even charities and non-government organisations to direct where supports are put."

title: Queensland council to turn park into a dedicated homeless camp
text:
A park in Moreton Bay will soon become a free, legal campsite for people experiencing homelessness under a 12-month trial by the local council.

Wyllie Park in Petrie is already an overnight camping area with toilets and refuse facilities, and will offer 60 free sites for those who cannot afford standard rent or caravan park fees.

The Moreton Bay Council says the precinct will be monitored by CCTV cameras and round-the-clock security.

In March, the Supreme Court ruled the local council violated the human rights of homeless campers when it evicted them from public parks in 2025.

Homeless campers will have access to toilets, bins, a barbecue, and running water at the park.

Peter Flannery says the camp is not a replacement for social housing. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Speaking to Ellen Fanning on 612 ABC Brisbane Drive, Mayor Peter Flannery says the trial will offer a centralised location where support services can easily support rough sleepers.

"Rather than being scattered across our whole city, let's get them into one location where they can be supported and have some safety," Cr Flannery said.

"We did learn from the court case that we shouldn't have asked them to move to somewhere when there was nowhere else to go, so this is providing that somewhere else to go."

Bandaid solution

Founder of Nourish Street, Beau Haywood, welcomes the announcement, but has genuine concerns about the trial.

Mr Haywood says he is unsure how the trial will address the complex needs of people experiencing homelessness.

"Homelessness is not a single group of people," he says.

"You could potentially have families with children, elderly people, people experiencing significant mental health issues, people battling addiction, vulnerable women all staying in one area."

Beau Haywood's charity feeds homeless people across Moreton Bay. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Mr Haywood says his charity, which provides essential supplies to rough sleepers in the area, was not consulted by council.

"We're one of the largest [charities] in this area. So, it was a bit disappointing once again that no-one was really sort of spoken to about what was happening or how it was going to be addressed," he says.

"I just sort of wonder if this is another council knee-jerk reaction."

Mr Haywood also raised concerns that the park limit of 60 sites will not be enough to support the region's accommodation needs.

Nourish Street's most recent food distribution run in Moreton Bay visited 174 sites.

"Simply providing somewhere for people to pitch a tent without adequate support, security and pathways into permanent housing risks creating another problem, whether they are solving one we already have."

title: Risky drinking persists in rural WA despite culture shift
text:
If Australians are thought to be heavy drinkers, the stereotype is even stronger for rural station and farm workers.

The cliche is supported by public health data showing higher rates of risky drinking in isolated regions, including Western Australia's north.

The Pilbara region, around 1,100km north of Perth, found 51 per cent of adults drank more than 10 standard drinks a week in 2024.

This is compared to 49.2 per cent further north in the Kimberley and 35.5 per cent across all of WA.

Prevalence estimate of high risk alcohol consumption by health region in Western Australia 2024. (Supplied: Epidemiology Directorate)

Alcohol use on cattle stations

Mark Bettini was 21 when his family took over De Grey Station near Port Hedland, about 1,700km north of Perth, in 1996.

He said factors like long days and social influence contributed to excessive alcohol consumption at the time.

"I think in the early days, alcohol was quite a big problem in our crew, and I won't pretend that I wasn't taking part in it," Mr Bettini said.

"When you are working long hours and you come back and you're tired, sometimes a beer becomes a real attraction.

"I think when you're using alcohol to relax, it's very hard to get out of that habit."

Pilbara pastoralist and general manager of Bettini Beef, Mark Bettini. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Remote workers more likely to drink heavily

National Drug Research Institute professor Nyanda McBride said rural and farming areas often had higher rates of hazardous drinking due to factors like stress and isolation.

"Some of the risk factors around that increase is being male, lower socio-economic status, and psychological problems such as depression," she said.

"But there's also financial stressors, seasonal stressors that come with farming, work-life balance, physical health, and disconnection."

Ms McBride said drinking alcohol was commonly used as a coping strategy.

Research shows risky alcohol consumption is more common in regional and remote areas. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

Coupled with this were barriers to accessing mental healthcare, such as physical distance, a lack of knowledge about treatment options, and traditional stoicism — the belief men must shoulder burdens alone.

Farmer Shanna Whan, who began her life on the land as a "baby jillaroo", said drinking culture in the bush was deeply ingrained.

At the station she worked after school, alcohol was the centrepiece of social life.

Ms Whan said this led to a "horrifying" experience.

"I was not in a safe environment, and alcohol was very prevalent," she said.

"By the end of my first year out of boarding school, I'd been sexually assaulted six different times … and alcohol was involved.

"It's a really sad story and I'm very sad to say also it's a very common story."

Ms Whan's consumption of alcohol increased while working in the agriculture sector and she believed the only way to do deals, make friends, or "fit in" was over a beer.

After two years of personal recovery, Ms Whan launched charity Sober in the Country with a goal to normalise saying no to alcohol in rural Australia.

She said the charity's advocacy over the past 12 years had contributed to "huge change" in rural and remote communities, particularly in how young people viewed alcohol — but there remained more work to be done.

Sober in the Country founder Shanna Whan AM is trying to break the stigma of saying no to alcohol in the bush. (Supplied: Shanna Whan)

Change is afoot

As manager of De Grey Station, Mr Bettini said there had been instances where crew members' alcohol use went too far.

"I've seen people drinking too much then trying to turn up for work still drunk and you have to stand them down," he said.

"We've had damage to the quarters and that sort of thing because people have drunk too many spirits.

"We had to ban spirits for a time or two because it's got out of hand — but in the last few years, we've not had to do that at all, which is fantastic."

Mr Bettini said he had recently noticed a "dramatic improvement" in the drinking habits of his new and young staff members, and their ability to say no to a drink.

"We just want to promote a safe workplace," he said.

"For me, the last 10 years, I've seen a dramatic improvement in young 17, 18, 19-year-olds coming into the workforce and having good habits to start with.

"Whatever's happening out there is great and it gives me a lot of hope and enthusiasm that the industry is going to be safe and strong.

"Probably we'll have a lot better leadership from those guys coming through."

title: Is having a romantic AI companion cheating? Some people think so
text:
What do you look for in a partner? Emotional support? Good listening skills? Romantic connection?

People are increasingly finding these traits in AI companions and turning to them even when in a committed — human — relationship.

But with romantic and even sexual intimacy possible between a user and AI, is it cheating?

"New studies show about half of people who are in a relationship with an AI companion are also in regular relationship, so it's not just a substitute, but also a complement," says Raffaele Ciriello, an expert in AI companions and digital relationships at the University of Sydney.

He says as an emerging type of relationship, it's up for debate if having an AI companion constitutes as cheating, "just like people debate if ethical non-monogamy can exist".

As the technology continues to evolve, sexologist and couples therapist Isiah McKimmie says people will be forced to continually ask themselves, is this OK for me and my relationship, or does this feel like a breach?

What makes AI companions appealing?

AI companions such as Replika and Character.AI are software programs that use conversation to mimic human-like relationships.

Researchers say creators of AI companion apps often market their chatbots in ways that humanise them, emphasising that qualities they present are "better" than those of human partners.

They offer constant availability and support, and "do not get tired or annoyed", the research reveals.

Dr Ciriello says it's that accessibility, and their ability to be personalised to a user's desires, that makes them so powerful.

"It's this adaptability and customisation that allows the user to feel understood and that they can get more tailored advice from AI than other technology, or even people."

Dr Ciriello says people use them for emotional and sexual purposes, which can feel "exciting and new".

"Novelty is doing a lot of the work … a lot of people are experimenting with this and because sexuality is such an important part of human life, of course people are using AI to explore it."

Ms McKimmie says AI companions are "fantastically appealing" because they are there any time you need them, "and don't come with their own needs".

"Sometimes real humans are too tired or stressed to be able to listen well, or just haven't learnt those skills, or have something going on for them they want to talk through, too.

"[AI] is all of the emotional support that we want, without having to give back."

What the data says

Relationship experts say what crosses the line in one relationship, might not in another. (Pexels: cottonbro studio)

Research from Canada found half of 1,815 people surveyed would consider a partner's romantic AI companion use as infidelity.

The authors said reactions to romantic companions were about as negative as reactions to dating apps and webcamming — both of which involve a human third party.

"They were more negative than reactions to all other sexual technologies, such as AI pornography and sex toys."

The research also found nearly two-thirds of AI romantic companion users kept it a secret.

Australia doesn't have similar data, but a YouGov study revealed one in seven Australians could imagine falling in love with an AI tool.

That rose to 28 per cent among gen Z respondents.

Ms McKimmie says what crosses the line in one relationship might not in another.

"I've worked with couples who came to me for what they call infidelity, for example one partner watching porn.

"For other couples that might be seen as normal, or expected, and even healthy."

Using AI chatbots for relationship advice While the accessibility and "judgement-free zone" of AI chatbots can be attractive when seeking relationship advice, experts warn there are risks you need to be aware of.

Pornography use is just one example. But Dr Ciriello says what sets AI companionship apart from other ethical issues with technology in relationships is sensitive relational disclosure.

"On a porn website you don't typically provide a lot of personal information about yourself, but with an AI companion, that is the whole point."

And some people will consider that a breach of trust or betrayal, he says.

"The fact people are talking about their relationship with AI means people are implicated that haven't necessarily consented to being part of that conversation.

"Sharing sensitive information about other people creates an ethical grey area that is not sufficiently addressed through existing privacy laws and regulations."

Have you found yourself forming a human-like relationship with AI? We'd love to hear from you

How to navigate AI companions in your relationship

Ms McKimmie says it's going to be up to each couple to work out expectations around AI use and come to an agreement on what's appropriate for the relationship.

"Really, it does require talking about it and working through it together as a team.

" We still need this very human ability to communicate when it comes to these issues. "

For those feeling hurt or insecure by their partner's AI companion use, Ms McKimmie suggests approaching the conversation with openness and curiosity, while also sharing your vulnerabilities around it.

"They understandably might be feeling lonely and not good enough … [and] like the relationship is unstable and insecure, and that is really scary."

Engaging a therapist can help navigate these conversations if you aren't making headway alone.

"Professional support can reveal underlying reasons why someone is turning to AI," Ms McKimmie says.

Depending on what your partner is using an AI companion for, Dr Ciriello says consent may also form part of that conversation.

"Relational consent is the biggest concern and probably the most legitimate objection people might have to these relationships."

title: Warning for mariners as ghost rig lights goes out
text:
An abandoned oil drilling rig rusting away at sea is now raising safety concerns now the platform's lights are no longer working.

The Cliff Head oil platform has been at the centre of a storm over who foots the $200 million clean up bill after junior oil and gas companies Pilot and Triangle energy entered voluntary administration.

Pilot was working with Triangle to repurpose the rig but in July both companies went bust.

Now sitting idle at sea 11 kilometres off the coast of Dongara, about 350 kilometres north of Perth, the rig which has been used as a navigation aid for over a decade remains unlit.

'Extremely dangerous'

The stretch of water where the old drilling rig sits is frequented by mariners including commercial fishermen.

Western Australia's Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure released an alert about the lack of lighting on the oil rig.

Marine Safety WA has advised all mariners in Dongara and Leeman waters to be aware of the 500 metre exclusion zone surrounding the site and to check navigation warnings.

Thomas Mayo says the unlit platform is very dangerous. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Maritime Union of Australia's assistant national secretary Thomas Mayo said unlit infrastructure out at sea can be a "huge risk for mariners" at night.

"It's very dark out there, you don't have street lights or anything like that [in the ocean]," he said.

"You've got all sorts of weather and conditions to contend with so it's extremely dangerous to have a facility out there unlit.

"These things should be cleaned up quickly after they've finished their time of production."

The Cliff Head platform sits abandoned offshore following the recent voluntary administration of operators Triangle Operations and Pilot Energy. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Calls for action

Since the future of the platform has been in doubt, the decommissioning process, including who will pay for it has not been made clear.

Federal resources minister Madeline King previously said "under no circumstances" would the taxpayer be responsible for footing the bill.

"In the event of companies being unable to pay I will have no hesitation in extending the Northern Endeavor levy or taking other measures to cover all costs of decommissioning," she said.

The Cliff Head platform has operated since 2006, but today it sits abandoned off the Dongara coastline. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But Mr Mayo said there needed to be "greater action".

"It's an indication of what we would possibly see more of because oil and gas companies are increasingly abandoning platforms like this and not following up with their obligations to do the clean-up after," he said.

"They certainly shouldn't be getting away [without decommissioning] and then putting mariners at danger."

A spokesperson for the administrators said they were aware of concerns regarding the rig's lighting.

Meanwhile a spokesperson for the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority said they were working to reduce hazards "imminently".

"NOPSEMA is aware the facility is currently unlit and is coordinating the deployment of navigational aids which includes lighting," they said.

"In the interim, information about the facility's location and status is available to mariners through navigational safety information issued by maritime authorities."

title: How a 1mm error had Supercars champ driving a slower car all season
text:
Supercars and Triple Eight Race Engineering have both responded after the revelation that 2024 champion Will Brown has been driving with an engine airflow restrictor that is 1 millimetre undersized all season.

Throughout 25 races in 2026, Brown has achieved one pole position and two podiums, while teammate Broc Feeney has five wins in what should be similar machinery.

But on Tuesday night, following a poor outing for Brown in Perth two weekends ago, Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering found Brown's Ford Mustang has been underpowered all season.

"After Perth we promised Will, his crew and all stakeholders associated with Car #888, which includes our beloved fans, that we would leave no stone unturned and find reasons why Car #888 has not been fighting for race wins recently," team principal Jamie Whincup said.

"At 7pm [Tuesday] night we found a significant issue on Car #888.

"Since the start of this season, Car #888 has been running with an undersized engine airflow restrictor. This part manages the airflow into the engine and has a significant negative impact on engine performance, and therefore lap time.

"This is not a part we, Triple Eight or Red Bull Ampol Racing, manufacture. This is a supplied part from Supercars expected to be the same for all 11 Ford Mustangs, distributed at the start of the season and expected to be run for the whole season."

Will Brown has just two podiums from 25 races this season. (Getty Images: Daniel Kalisz)

Whincup said the undersized part was costing Brown 0.15 seconds per lap, explaining why the Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering driver has struggled for pace often this year.

"We as a team are taking responsibility and want to deeply apologise to everyone involved for allowing this to happen," Whincup said.

"While this error has cost our team a considerable amount of resource, sport is an emotional game and these types of things have knock-on effects bigger than the average 1.5 tenths a lap.

"We will be taking up with Supercars why they have supplied us with what is a controlled component out of specification, which has negatively impacted the performance of Car #888 this season to date.

"We will continue to roll out our new chassis for Car #888 at Queensland Raceway and look forward to measuring our capability now we are competing with the same horsepower as the rest of the field."

On Wednesday, Supercars acknowledged the revelation that Will Brown's car had been fitted with an air restrictor, provided by them, that was 1mm too small.

However, Supercars said the undersized restrictor was only supposed to be used for demonstration purposes only, provided for the team to do a launch in Geelong in February.

"The component was loaned by Supercars to Triple Eight Race Engineering (T8RE) for demonstration purposes only at the team's launch in February.

"The air restrictor subsequently remained fitted to Car 888 through the Perth Super 440. Neither party identified the discrepancy until it was discovered by T8RE during preparations for next weekend's event in Ipswich.

"Throughout the Supercars season, routine scrutineering and compliance checks are carried out at random by Supercars' technical department, covering a vast range of components and systems. As of the Perth event, the air restrictor fitted to Car 888 had not been selected for inspection during those checks.

"Supercars is reviewing the circumstances surrounding this matter and will evaluate opportunities to strengthen its technical and operational procedures moving forward.

"Supercars acknowledges and appreciates T8RE's identifying and prompt reporting of the matter to Supercars."

Brown will now be driving with an engine on parity with the other Mustangs during the next round at Queensland Raceway in Ipswich on August 21-23.

title: Remote school bus axed leaving students and families stranded
text:
Hailed as a remote success story, Queensland's longest school bus service has been axed, leaving six primary students stranded from their school.

For the last six years, up to 18 students in the remote towns of Bidunggu and Gregory, about 300 kilometres north of Mount Isa, have made the three-hour daily return trip to Burketown State School to learn alongside peers in the classroom.

But during the last school holidays, Bidunggu resident and parent Natalie King said families were told the bus service would not resume in term three, leaving boarding school or School of the Air as the only educational options.

The next nearest primary school from Gregory is 165km away at Doomadgee, but there is no school bus.

"This bus gave them a chance to be with teachers in person … for students to have that kind of normal school experience," Ms King said.

"These kids need an education."

The wheels are coming off

The bus service was established in 2021 after Burketown State School approached the community to create a regular bus service and boost enrolments, which, according to the Department of Education, currently sit around 27 students.

Ms King said the 240km round trip each day was not ideal but resulted in far better outcomes than remote schooling.

"I sent my young fellow away to boarding school in Cairns after he graduated from Burketown. The teachers down there couldn't believe how well educated he was," she said.

"That's the sort of education we were getting."

The lengthy bus ride is 120km long, or roughly 90 minutes. (ABC North West Qld: Emily Dobson)

The service was funded by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) and was operated by Burketown State School until last term.

Burketown State School declined to comment.

A Queensland Department of Education spokesperson said the state school had worked hard to try and find a replacement operator.

"The Department of Education is working closely with the principal to identify any eligible drivers within the school community; however, the very limited availability of suitably qualified drivers and staff absences have impacted the continuity of the bus service," the spokesperson said.

"The Mount Isa School of the Air is liaising with the three families and six students to engage in further education.

"We will continue to liaise with TMR, who are investigating if there are any options for the bus to be run by the council or other community-based groups."

A TMR spokesperson confirmed funding was available for the service, but no replacement had been found so far.

Calls for a school

Monique Mckerrell's family fell in love with the area on a cross-country road trip. (Supplied: Monique Mckerrell)

Gregory resident Monique Mckerrell moved to the region with her two children after being amazed by the area's natural beauty.

"We were planning on travelling Australia … we found Gregory and fell in love," she said.

"The spring that runs all year round to swim in, fish in, there's lots of hunting that we enjoy doing too, it was just prime."

Monique Mckerrell fears that as her children get older they will miss out on the same schooling and social experience other kids receive. (Supplied: Monique Mckerrell)

But the bus service's closure has raised questions about what future is possible in a town without access to face-to-face schooling.

"Going to school is an important life experience, learning how to be part of the world, communicating, listening, thinking, and trying new things, and then gaining that confidence away from home," she said.

"If you had a school [in Gregory], it would bring more people in the community … in the long run I would prefer a physical school in town."

Gregory previously had a primary school — a campus of Doomadgee State School — between 2003 and 2012, which closed after enrolments dwindled to four students.

But the community has grown.

According to the most recent census data, Gregory has a population of 122 people, about 60 per cent more than the 2016 census.

Meanwhile, Burketown, where the region's only school remains, recorded a population of 204 people in 2021, down 34 residents from 2016

Ms King agreed a school at Gregory was needed as raising children without access to face-to-face learning was "too hard".

"It's just so sad because a lot of families, they want to come home, they want to come back … but now that we've got no school it's too hard."

A Department of Education spokesperson said little evidence supported the construction of a new school in the Gregory area.

Natalie King said the school bus service gave students a chance to play, socialise and learn face-to-face. (ABC North West Qld: Emily Dobson)

"When planning for new schools, the department considers a broad range of factors to establish a service need to provide a new school," the spokesperson said.

"For most new schools in Queensland, the service need is underpinned by an analysis of the local school network and its ability to meet projected population growth."
