title: Wall Street is about to sell AI bonds. What could go wrong?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessBanking & financeAI Opinion Wall Street is about to sell AI bonds. What could go wrong? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 13, 2026 — 12:16pm

August 13, 2026 — 12:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What do you do when your financial capacity to help your customers buy your products becomes stretched? You turn to Wall Street, of course. That’s what Nvidia has done, enlisting some of the biggest names in private capital – Goldman Sachs, Apollo Global, KKR, Brookfield and Black Rock – to arrange a pool of $US500 billion ($708 billion) or more of capital to help fund purchases of Nvidia chips. Nvidia needs money - and Wall Street is keen to provide it. Bloomberg The firms haven’t actually committed that much capital – they’ve signed memorandums of understanding, not lines of credit – and every project brought before them will be individually evaluated. Nevertheless, Wall Street has provided a signal of intent.

Advertisement

With Nvidia’s own ability to continue to effectively provide vendor financing for purchases of its chips – the “circular financing” arrangements that have been increasingly scrutinised and criticised – perhaps constrained, it wants to enlarge that circle – and it’s Wall Street’s access to vast pools of private capital that will enable that. Not that Nvidia won’t contribute. It says it will guarantee 25 per cent of the residual value of the collateral for any project. For the Wall Street firms, the allure is that it could create a new class of asset-backed securities that they can on-sell to pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and wealthy investors, clipping the tickets on the way through. The company refers to those projects – the chips and data centres and other infrastructure that support the training of AI models – as “AI factories,” but two-thirds or more of the value of those factories will lie in the value of its own chips. That’s potentially a $US125 billion exposure for Nvidia, its shareholders and creditors. For Nvidia, the concept is designed to increase the capacity of its non-hyperscaler customers to fund the purchases of its chips.

Advertisement

Sharemarkets and conventional lenders have become warier, and more discerning, about the AI companies they are prepared to back now that the hyperscalers are out-spending their cashflows and competing for equity and debt. The cost of equity and debt for the smaller entities is becoming prohibitive. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The AI spending frenzy is giving investors anxiety Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist For the Wall Street firms, the allure of the concept is that it could create a new class of asset-backed securities that they can on-sell to pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and wealthy investors, clipping the tickets, naturally, on the way through. The “AI factories,” are, however, rather different to the asset classes that are usually securitised. The cash flows from securitised residential and commercial mortgages, or infrastructure assets, or corporate loans are high quality and supported by cashflows and collateral that tend to increase in value over time.

Advertisement

The core assets of the AI factories, the Nvidia chips, have more limited and uncertain lifespans. The income streams they might generate and their value as collateral is less certain, but almost certainly diminishes over time. There’s a debate about the useful lives of chips, given that Nvidia (and others) produces a “next generation” chip with superior capabilities every two years or so. Some argue that their value should be fully depreciated over only three to five years. Nvidia says their useful life can be up to a decade. There’s no doubt, however, that an outdated chip whose use is now to apply the knowledge gained from the training of AI models is less valuable than the latest generation chips being used to train those models. The decline in value over time – and the time period is unknowable today – would erode the value of the collateral, with Nvidia’s guarantee providing the backstop for investors.

Advertisement

What Nvidia and its Wall Street are depicting is a form of collateralised debt, with Nvidia holding the “first loss” tranche that will be called on if a loan defaults and the rate of chip obsolescence is greater than anticipated. With Nvidia’s own ability to provide vendor financing for purchases of its chips constrained, it wants to access Wall Street’s vast pools of private capital. Bloomberg Wall Street is good at financial engineering a solution to difficult financial challenges and, faced with funding the biggest investment boom in history, there’s no bigger challenge than supplying the capital to acquire the chips and infrastructure for artificial intelligence. It’s not just the scale of the demand for capital – the hyperscalers ( Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) alone are investing about $US750 billion, largely in AI, this year and will spend more than $US1 trillion next year -- but the reality is that AI revenue growth is being far outstripped by the growth rate of the spending. It appears near certain that those hyperscalers, despite their vast legacy cashflows, will all be cash-negative, and more highly leveraged, next year.

Advertisement

Google has raised new equity and most of the big tech companies pursuing AI leadership ambitions have, perhaps for the first time, begun tapping debt markets, with about $US350 billion of AI-related bond issues so far this year. Despite the cash from their non-AI businesses, the spreads on those bonds have been blowing out. Wall Street firms can be ingenious but, as the global financial crisis demonstrated, they sometimes push the risk envelope too far. Independent AI promoters like OpenAI and Anthropic have raised their capital from private investors and are, like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, planning initial public offerings to access the bigger pool of equity capital in the listed market. Any debt they have raised – and SpaceX has raised debt – would be priced as “junk” and be costly. At those companies’ rates of investment, however – and the market’s satiation with all things AI – the planned listings might provide a bandaid, not a cure, for their financial stress. At face value, gaining access to the estimated $US22 trillion of private capital could provide the extra funding required, and provide it on more attractive/less expensive terms than are currently available to individual AI borrowers.

Advertisement

Securitising debts – packaging up parcels of loans and therefore diversifying the risks – would create securities with much stronger credit quality than that of an individual AI borrower. As was discovered in 2008 and the sub-prime mortgage crisis, however, bundling poor credits together doesn’t necessarily alter the reality that they are risky loans that could all go south together. Related Article Opinion

AI Scared by tech’s debt deluge, investors are questioning the AI boom Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist As the Nvidia chips age, the value of the collateral that the end-investors holding those bundles rely on would be diminishing. And even that diminished value would be vulnerable as inference chips become increasingly commoditised. That’s the segment of the sector – the applications of AI – that China is strategically targeting, with chips whose prices already significantly undercut their US counterparts. The collateral, in the event of a default, could be near-worthless.

Advertisement

The Wall Street firms are no doubt comforted by Nvidia’s guarantee, but the tech giant is at the epicentre of the boom in AI and AI valuations and has – due to its myriad of circular financing deals in a sector where there are now layers of circularity to financial relationships – a leveraged exposure to the fate of that boom. The degree of financial engineering already pervasive in the sector and the extent to which the off-balance-sheet liabilities of AI’s blue-chip companies, estimated at more than $US1.6 trillion, now surpass their debt on the balance sheet, say that all the conventional funding options for AI in the US have been stretched to their limits. In a sense, the agreement Nvidia unveiled with the Wall Street players underscores how fragile the AI ecosystem now is. Unable to raise sufficient funds conventionally, the sector is being forced to turn to a bespoke, unconventional, financially engineered structure to try to sustain its insatiable appetite for risk capital. Wall Street firms can be ingenious but, as the global financial crisis demonstrated, they sometimes push the risk envelope too far, with unpleasant consequences.

Advertisement

title: I signed up for the outback’s Squid Game. Now I look like a gaudy octopus
text:

LifestyleLife & relationshipsThe Kimberley Opinion I signed up for the outback’s Squid Game. Now I look like a gaudy octopus Far from the comforts of home, I found something more consoling. Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age August 13, 2026 — 11:53am

August 13, 2026 — 11:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A veteran of the country’s north-west once told me, “You come out of the Kimberley to recover.” He was right. Everything in that gargantuan rockery is anathema to a modern human’s comfort, the place is a Thoreauvian sequence of Squid Game. I have so many welts, bites, stings, abrasions and bruises covering me that I look like a trespasser brought down by birdshot before being flogged. The pharmaceuticals are useless; swellings flicker and flare floridly across my hide like the bioluminescence on certain gaudy octopus that pulse and shimmer when goaded by a shark or an Attenborough. To walk the wild Kimberley is to make innumerable staccato decisions – where to step, which piece of stone might tip you headfirst into a sandstone crevasse garnished with spinifex? Which route will lead into a tangle of vine and elephant grass? Which into head-high spinifex and a barrage of eager green ants? Even camel hate spinifex, each plant a supernova of spines containing toxins to inflame, blister and infect your skin. Photo: Robin Cowcher Every day at walk’s end I used a hunting knife to lever ticks from my crevices as if I were a carpenter prising roofing nails from tin ... and then whisky to aid sleep on rock, of course, always rock, amid the screech and wing beat of bats as big as corgis. We were as remote as any place on today’s planet. On a plateau overlooking a wild river we found a cave mouth shaped like a gaping wound in a rock face three metres above the ground. Climbing to it, we found inside a conch shell the size of a football. Its patterns had faded to white.

Advertisement

How many years had it been here, carried two days’ walk from the sea – 200? 20,000? Had it been traded? How had it been got from the water among the massive crocodiles at this river’s mouth? Shells are as beautiful as flowers, but rarer and less ephemeral. This one must have been a treasure to its owners, likely handed from one keeper to the next through generations. Related Article Opinion

Celebrity life There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age The cave looked down on an amphitheatre of orange stone, its pillars and protrusions decorated with ceremonial figures the colour of dried blood. They were leaping and dancing, dressed in feathered skirts, elbow and knee bands and massive feathered headdresses like stooks of hay. It was as fine a place for ceremony as anything wrought by Christopher Wren. As I turned the huge shell in my hands it occurred to me that it was a musical instrument, as sonically profound and elemental to an ancient liturgy as a church organ, sitting there in the wall. And I suppose the figures dancing on the stone were dancing to notes once blown from this exotic instrument by some excited musician, some hopeful composer smiling as he brought the thing to his lips, some Amadeus delighted to watch the folk lose themselves in his notes, happily leading them on to abandon. The amphitheatre came alive for me and I could see the leaping shadows flickering in the firelight on the stone walls and hear the many singers, their voices echoing off the rock back into the dance in a feedback loop that must have sounded like affirmation from the pertinent spirits, freeing the whole on to higher enchantment.

Advertisement

Parents hefted toddlers aloft in the dance, larger children mimicked the moves of the cooler adults, old folk sat at the dance’s edge not wanting to dull the exuberance with their limited footwork, but smiling, approving, occasionally shouting encouragement. I imagined the whole corroboree as a kind of ecstatic gospel service in one of those churches in the US South that birth famous musicians, famous music and unparallelled emotion. All of it enabled by this conch shell I held in my hands, this invaluable gastropod trumpet blown by a barefoot Dizzy Gillespie. Ancient Aboriginal art in the Kimberley. I hefted the conch and lifted it towards my mouth, thinking I might attempt some antique note, some brief replication of a sound the blood dark figures on the walls might recognise and come alive to. But I didn’t do it. Nor would I pull the stops on a pipe organ in a deconsecrated church. We climbed up and put the conch back in the cave on the stone where we found it. It sits there in a place once central, sacred, now remote, an inanimate thing suffused with ghostly history and wondrous potential, like a church organ awaiting an organist and congregation that will never come again. title: Low-income Australians should accept substandard homes, Liberal frontbencher says
text:
in brief Liberals are this week pushing for a reduced housing code, which could streamline construction at the cost of quality.

Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg conceded that the proposal would come with "trade-offs".

The Coalition's plan to boost housing stock will involve "trade-offs", a Liberal frontbencher has said, after suggesting low-income households should accept living in substandard homes.

Opposition housing and homelessness spokesperson Andrew Bragg announced on Wednesday that the Opposition would reduce the national housing code from 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.

When asked by ABC Radio National on Thursday morning whether his policy means low-income earners should just accept living in substandard housing, he replied: "Yes, definitely."

He went on to say that building more homes under a streamlined code would come with "trade-offs".

"It's more important to have a house than to not have a house. And so, given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system, we need to just build more houses," he told the ABC.

Bragg's comments follow remarks made by his Liberal colleague and treasury spokesman Tim Wilson, who suggested in some cases people could put "a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money" on improving housing quality.

He told ABC RN on Wednesday there should not be a one-size-fits-all policy — such as mandated energy efficiency — for construction.

"There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it's not necessary," he said.

"We have a risk that Australians can't afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government's own budget design. We need housing stock that meets different needs in different environmental conditions. Queensland is not the same as Tasmania or Victoria. Western Australia is different again."

Proposal does 'nothing to fix' housing crisis, advocate says

Affordable housing advocates told SBS News that stripping back construction regulations is a way for developers to profit from "unliveable" homes.

"Too many renters are already living in homes that are freezing in winter, stifling in summer, riddled with mould and damp, and expensive to heat and cool," Everybody's Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said in a statement.

"Older people and people with disability already struggle to find homes they can safely and comfortably live in."

Azize added that the government should focus on social housing that is "built to last".

"We have a housing crisis because people cannot afford a home. Building more poor-quality homes does nothing to fix that crisis. It simply gives developers another way to profit from it," Azize said.

Australian Council of Social Services CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie agreed, adding that construction of social housing should "drastically scale up".

She described Bragg's comments as shocking.

"The changes to the building code proposed by Senator Bragg would simply remove costs from the builder and move them onto the household - locking them into higher power bills for decades, deepening inequality, risking lives, leaving future generations with homes that are expensive to run," she told SBS News.

The Housing Industry Association on Wednesday welcomed Senator Bragg's announcement, but argued it was more important to disentangle layers of complexity than target a specific size of the code.

Cutting red tape

The national housing codes set minimum requirements for the safety, health, amenity, accessibility, and sustainability of certain buildings, as detailed in over 2,000 pages.

The Coalition's new standards will focus on cost-effective structural, fire safety and health-related building standards.

Bragg said reducing the code has been a shifting policy for the Coalition.

"This was in Angus Taylor's budget reply back in May, and we have committed to getting it to 200 pages, but we actually found a way to get it to less than 100 pages. It tends to be by picking up the New Zealand building code, which is about 80," he explained.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil has dismissed earlier calls to reduce construction standards to 200 pages. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

While New Zealand's building code appears to be about 80 pages long, the country has other compulsory building requirements on durability and energy efficiency, outlined in separate documents that builders must comply with.

Labor announced it would freeze the National Construction Code following its productivity roundtable in mid-2026.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil brushed off calls from the Coalition to cut the construction standards to 200 pages earlier in 2026.

"I've talked to builders about that, they laugh their heads off. That is absolutely ridiculous," O'Neil told the National Press Club in May.

The government is not far off presenting a final plan to the building minister later this year to streamline the code, Treasurer Jim Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Wednesday.

Bragg has also called for the creation of a federal pattern book of model homes that could receive automatic approval from the states and territories.

title: A melon, or a message? The prized fruit at the centre of the Albanese controversy
text:
in brief The melons gifted to Anthony Albanese by the Japanese prime minister hold cultural significance.

Albanese's discussion of the gift has prompted accusations of cultural faux pas and disrespect.

As Anthony Albanese's weeks-old comments about melons continue to fuel political drama, the fruit at the centre of the controversy has largely been overlooked.

Yet the crown melons gifted to the prime minister by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are no ordinary fruit.

In Japan, they are among the country's most prized gifts.

During an appearance on Nikki Osborne's Deep Bush podcast last month, Albanese described the melons as a "pretty strange" gift before praising their quality.

Hand gestures he made while discussing the fruit have since drawn criticism, an interpretation his office has rejected.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But what exactly did Takaichi's gift represent?

What are crown melons?

Both the fruit and gift-giving hold deep significance in Japanese culture.

Waka Ikeda, writing in the Japan Times, describes a crown melon as "perfection, based on the Japanese artisan spirit of takumi" — something you bring when you wish to honour someone. Her op-ed highlighting Albanese's comments on the podcast kickstarted the furore that has spilled over onto the international stage

Gwyn McClelland, senior lecturer in Japanese studies and president of the Japanese Studies Association of Australia, told SBS News that he shared the Japan Times story with his students to express how "incensed" he was by the prime minister's gesture.

His students were "also quite embarrassed", he said.

"I was just really annoyed that he didn't realise the giving of fruit could be really lovely and important," he said.

"In an Australian context, that doesn't look like an amazing gift, necessarily ... [but] I was upset that Albanese hadn't thought about gift-giving culture because it is very central in Japan.

"For me, the faux pas was really not taking the gift-giving seriously."

However, even for Japanese people, social etiquette around giving and receiving gifts is not straightforward. Eri Dennis, former officer at the Australian embassy in Tokyo and current cultural consultant at manufacturing consultancy Shinka Management, told SBS News the practice is deeply ingrained and "definitely an important part of our culture".

"Whenever we visit someone, even a family member or your friend, for some significant occasion, or if you haven't met them for some time, it's just a natural part of our culture that we bring along gifts," she said. "It doesn't have to be an expensive gift, but it's a gesture that we care about you."

Shizuoka Crown Melons are considered by some in Japan as closer to an art form than a fruit. Much like champagne, the "king of fruit" can only be produced in the Shizuoka prefecture on the south coast, grown in raised beds, hand-pollinated, and massaged to improve their look and sweetness.

Dennis notes that melons — grown throughout Japan with varieties tied to each prefecture — are associated with wealth and considered a "very expensive fruit". Typically, a valuable melon would be presented as a gift with ornate wrapping and placed in a special box.

"Japanese people, we enjoy the beauty of fleeting nature," he said, noting that gifts from nature are also tied up in aspects of Shinto Buddhist cultural understanding.

Shizuoka Crowns have a clean, highly concentrated honey-like flavour and a melt-in-your-mouth texture. Eating them is generally a communal act, shared between the family of those who have been presented with the melon, once it has been chilled in the fridge and the guest has long departed.

Sanae Takaichi brought the melons from Shizuoka for Anthony Albanese in May to mark the relaxation of Australian import standards, allowing their sale in Australia. Source: Supplied / X/@takaichi_sanae

Dennis explains that the agricultural industry has significant sway in Japanese politics and that a gift of fruit or vegetables is also seen as a way to honour the farmers who laboured to produce it. With each region boasting particular types of produce cultivation, regional and national pride stems from the growers themselves.

Yosuke Suzuki, a senior official at Shizuoka Prefecture Greenhouse Agricultural Cooperative, which has been producing Shizuoka Crown Melons since 1921, told SBS News that their cultivation techniques have been passed down through generations.

"One of the distinctive features of our melons is a cultivation method known as "ichiboku ikka" — one fruit per plant. We grow just one melon on each plant, so all the nutrients are concentrated into that single fruit. That allows us to produce an exceptionally delicious melon," he said.

Crown melons are a type of muskmelon, which are so called because they have been bred to omit a fragrant odour that fills the room when cut. They are graded for their appearance and prized for their T-shaped stems, with the most symmetrical melons fetching eye-watering sums at auction.

In 2019, a pair of Yubari King melons grown in Hokkaido sold for ¥5 million ($44,400). More typically, top-grade melons retail for upwards of $300.

"It isn’t just about the taste. We also place great importance on their appearance. The netting pattern on the surface is beautifully and evenly distributed. That is the result of the tremendous care producers put into each melon, tending to them every single day," Suzuki added.

Fruits, like these Yubari melons, have become regional symbols and are gifted as a source of local pride or inter-cultural exchange. They can fetch high prices at auction. This pair sold for ¥3 million ($26,600) in 2024. Source: AFP / Yosuke Hayasaka

Takaichi brought the melons from Shizuoka for Albanese in May in celebration of the Australian import standards being relaxed to allow their sale here. Suzuki notes that his company are targeting 3,000 melons for sale on the domestic market.

High-end Japanese restaurants have already received the first batch of Shizuoka Crowns, according to Japanese media; however, SBS News could not locate any of the recipient restaurants and was told by one high-end importer that they were unaware of the rule change.

On Wednesday, the Opposition referred the issue to the Australian Federal Police, which confirmed to SBS News that it has received correspondence about confidential communications via Japanese official channels.

Dennis doesn't believe that Albanese "did anything wrong", although she can see how describing the gift as "strange" could be seen as disrespectful to some.

"Maybe the older generation might think 'how rude', but I think it's just part of cultural exchange and we move on," she said.

That said, she expects the incident has been an incredible boost to the Japanese melon industry and expects that many Australians will be eager to try the fruit that has caused such a fuss.

title: New Zealand PM Chris Luxon survived a leadership fight, but a greater challenge lies ahead
text:
In brief New Zealand prime minister Chris Luxon survived a leadership fight on Wednesday.

It followed a series of recent gaffes and mis-steps as his National party looks to November's general election.

Chris Luxon will box on as New Zealand prime minister after winning a caucus confidence vote, defying doubters in and outside his party after a run of gaffes that imperilled his premiership.

The National leader called a crunch meeting of his partyroom for Wednesday morning to end speculation around his future.

A leadership change looked on after NZ Herald reported growing dissatisfaction with Luxon's performance, three months out from the 7 November election.

Instead, Luxon emerged victorious from the lengthy meeting, claiming to have united the party and pledging to win a second term for his conservative coalition.

"There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus," he said, in a 75-second appearance without taking questions.

"Now we're going back to work, and we're moving on."

Luxon's office later revealed low-profile defence minister Chris Penk challenged for the leadership in the meeting.

The prime minister then sacked him for doing so, leaving Penk to announce his intention to leave politics at the November election.

Wednesday's vote followed a similar caucus showdown in April, when Luxon brought on and won a confidence vote to silence his critics.

The margin of each vote is a tightly held secret, though media outlets have reported the April result was 27-22 in Luxon's favour.

Rather than Penk, Wellington newspaper The Post reported Erica Stanford, the education minister, was the most likely challenger.

The 48-year-old never confirmed this, and was served a brutal backhander by colleague Nicola Grigg, the minister for women, on the way to the meeting.

"She's a good friend of mine, but she's not a prime minister," Grigg said.

Most observers tipped a successful spill.

One political editor described Luxon's leadership as "hanging by a thread" on Tuesday night, and another rated his survival as "incredibly unlikely", making his victory a defiant and triumphant moment for Luxon.

How did Luxon find himself in this position?

Mentored by party messiah John Key, the 56-year-old former Air New Zealand chief executive enjoyed a meteoric rise in politics.

He entered parliament in 2020, became opposition leader in 2021 and won the 2023 election.

However, he has endured a tough run in the top job, failing to deliver on key campaign pledges to improve New Zealand's misfiring economy and tackle government waste.

His corporate communication style is routinely mocked, and his poor personal popularity is widely seen as a key reason behind National's plunging poll fortunes, from 38 per cent at the election, to a poll average of 29 per cent.

A run of recent gaffes brought about the second leadership vote.

Luxon told battling small business owners in Rotorua they were "negative" and should instead be "retooling and radically disrupting your business".

READ MORE 'Shameful': Outrage as New Zealand scraps its standalone environment department

He also defended his use of a defence force plane to fly home after a party fundraiser — a shocking look for a leader who was forced to return a housing entitlement to stay at his own mortgage-free property.

Luxon has also been pushed around by NZ First leader and foreign minister Winston Peters, who in July caused outrage by telling a China-born Greens MP to "go back to your own country" in parliament.

While Luxon said the 81-year-old maverick's comment was racist, he did not sanction or sack him.

Despite the drama, the National-led coalition remains on course to win re-election on 7 November.

While the contest is tight, the right bloc has consistently kept an edge over the left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, also known as the Māori Party.

The race has been challenged in recent months by the emergence of newcomer party Opportunity, which hit eight per cent support in a TVNZ poll released on Wednesday.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the leadership shenanigans showed National was in disarray.

"New Zealanders have had a gutful of politicians fighting amongst themselves ... at a time when New Zealanders need them to be fighting for them," he said.

title: 'We're not asking for an easy life': The three key issues at the heart of Australia's 'polycrisis'
text:
IN BRIEF Experts say housing insecurity and climate fears are compounding young Australians' uncertainty about their future.

Young people's belief they can create change improved after the 2025 federal election, a recent report found.

For 24-year-old Sophie Blach, the future feels increasingly difficult to plan.

Working full-time hours in retail and hospitality while undertaking her degree, she said she has been forced to return to her Brisbane family home while she tries to save a deposit to eventually buy a property.

But rising everyday costs mean saving is difficult, leaving her feeling as though the traditional path into adulthood is becoming increasingly out of reach.

"I feel like I'm doing everything you're told you're supposed to do. I'm working, I'm studying, I'm saving when I can," she told SBS News.

"But I wouldn't say my goals feel in reach."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Young Australians are struggling to plan for the future

Sophie's experience reflects a broader trend identified in a new five-year analysis of the Australian Youth Barometer.

The Monash Centre for Youth Policy and Education Practice has tracked more than 2,700 Australians aged 18 to 24 since 2021, examining their experiences across work, education, housing, wellbeing, relationships and civic participation.

READ MORE The surprising factor shaping young Australians' family plans

Its latest report describes young Australians as living through a "polycrisis" of overlapping economic, social, environmental and political pressures that compound one another.

Affordable housing was the biggest issue young people flagged as needing urgent action, rising from 60 per cent in 2022 to 82 per cent in 2025.

Also recognised as needing urgent action was employment opportunities, which rose from 48 in 2022 to 64 per cent in 2025. Climate change was identified as an issue needing urgent action by 44 per cent in 2025, falling from 47 per cent in 2022.

Monash University professor Lucas Walsh, the report's lead author, says the significance of the findings is in how those issues connect.

"These are all embedded within the idea of a polycrisis, which involves overlapping independent events in crisis that intersect and amplify each other," he told SBS News.

Walsh said the study started tracking young Australians at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, providing a five-year window into how their lives and priorities have changed as the country moved through and beyond it.

He describes the pandemic as a "flash of light into more persistent problems" which exposed pressures that were already disproportionately affecting young people.

For Sophie, housing uncertainty isn't isolated from the rest of her life.

Housing and financial pressure are compounding

"I don't necessarily expect to own a house tomorrow, but I would like to feel like it's something I could realistically work towards. It can be discouraging to feel like the goalposts for how much I need to have saved, how much I need to be earning or even spending to get a home keeps changing," she said.

Wendy Stone, a professor of housing and social policy at Swinburne University, told SBS News that secure housing provides the foundation that young people need to establish independence, work, study and relationships.

But she said Australia's housing system is increasingly failing to provide that security, which can affect whether young people can sustain employment or education and even their ability to plan ahead.

"The affordability problem compounds other parts of our system's structural challenges for young people," stone said.

"One of the things that we do know is that the earlier you can get into a secure housing situation, the more likely you are to be able to pursue your education, your employment and your relationships in a way that is sustainable."

Stone said governments need to treat secure, affordable housing as an investment in young people, rather than relying on increased housing supply alone.

She points to targeted housing subsidies for young people undertaking study or training, alongside stronger protections and incentives for long-term renting.

The pressures are also being felt in young people's mental health, with the Barometer finding 99 per cent of the young Australians surveyed reported at least one feeling of anxiety or pessimism in 2025.

Meanwhile, the proportion who sought and received mental-health support fell from 31 per cent in 2021 to 23 per cent in 2025.

Professor of psychiatry Ian Hickie said much of the distress being experienced by young people is connected to practical pressures in their everyday lives.

"A lot of distress is being expressed by young people at the moment has to do with these broader sets of issues that are confronting them on a daily basis," he said.

He said solutions need to be practical measures, from reducing transport costs and providing rental assistance to improving access to health and other essential services.

Climate change adding another layer

Sydney University research fellow Scarlett Smout said young people can feel particularly powerless because they have been "failed by generations preceding them" and now feel they have inherited a problem they have little individual power to solve.

She told SBS News that effective solutions need to create connection and agency, including better access to nature, public transport and community spaces, while making clear that responsibility cannot rest on individuals alone.

"Seeing the government address climate change as a matter of inter-generational inequality but also inter-generational fairness … would hopefully provide some assurance to young people that this matter is being taken seriously and not just the can being kicked down the road."

For Sophie, her concerns can feel inseparable.

"I don't think we're asking for an easy life. We just want to believe that if we work hard, we'll have some control over what happens next," she said.

"In my parents' generation it was more simple, so I didn't think I would be making all these sacrifices and doing all the right things and still not have any reprieve or certainty over what my future will look like. It's demotivating."

Walsh urged governments to respond to these overlapping issues by breaking down siloed policy approaches and, crucially, giving young people a meaningful role in shaping the policies that affect them.

Bleak but not hopeless

The Barometer also found that young people's belief that change is possible improved following the 2025 federal election.

But for Sophie, that hope remains conditional.

"I recognise the privilege we have here in Australia and I do believe there are ways to fix the problems people in my generation are concerned about," she said.

"I try to stay optimistic; it would just help if there was a bit more to be hopeful about, or if it felt like my generation's concerns were actually being prioritised or even considered."

title: A new era for Australia's gig workers? The changes coming for delivery drivers
text:
IN BRIEF On-demand food delivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 per hour in Australia.

The changes will take effect from 17 August and have been praised by the Transport Workers' Union.

The Fair Work Commission has issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers, including on-demand food, beverage and grocery delivery drivers.

The standards, released on Tuesday, stipulate that on-demand delivery workers must be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 or up to $32 per hour, depending on the type of vehicle used. The order also specifies that delivery platforms must insure workers for on-the-job injuries.

The Transport Workers' Union (TWU), which represents Australian gig workers, said these changes have been years in the making. The TWU initially applied for the minimum standards order in 2024, alongside food delivery platforms Uber Eats and DoorDash.

In a joint statement provided to SBS News, TWU national secretary Michael Kaine described the new standards as "world-leading".

"The world is looking on as gig workers in Australia win new rights and protections that will change their lives, after years of campaigning for a better industry," Kaine said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth also believes the order is a "big step" in providing more robust worker protections.

She said it means "food and delivery workers don't have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections".

The new standards are set to start on Monday 17 August.

Who is covered by the order?

The TWU said "hundreds of thousands" of delivery workers in Australia will be impacted by the new orders.

They specifically apply to employee-like workers who are engaged through digital on-demand delivery platforms — such as Uber Eats and DoorDash — and mainly deliver consumables (food, beverages or liquor) or supermarket groceries.

These workers will be entitled to a guaranteed minimum hourly rate for their "engaged time" between accepting an order and completing the delivery. This is also called an "earnings floor".

People operating bicycles or e-bikes will be paid $31.30 an hour. For motorbikes, this increases to $31.80 per hour, and workers driving cars will earn $32 per hour.

According to the interim order, platforms will calculate a worker's total earnings over a period of up to 21 days. If a worker "has been paid less than the earnings floor in an earnings period, the digital labour platform operator will pay a top-up amount to ... make up the difference", it said.

Right to unpaid time away

The standards also aim to provide a clearer dispute resolution process and workers the right to (unpaid) time away. Key provisions include:

Platforms will establish a feedback forum to enable workers to raise questions or concerns about their work.

If an issue is unable to be resolved between the worker and delivery platform, drivers can refer the dispute to the Fair Work Commission.

Delivery drivers can choose to take "time away" from work without pay.

Time away is at the discretion of workers.

Maggie Lloyd, DoorDash's head of public policy for the Asia-Pacific, Central Asia and the Middle East, described these changes as a "defining moment" for Australia's on-demand economy.

"These new standards prove that strong worker protections and the flexibility that delivery workers value can go hand in hand," Lloyd said in a statement.

Insurance changes

Under the standards, delivery drivers will be responsible for taking out and maintaining compulsory third-party insurance for any vehicles used to provide services. They must also inform their insurer that the vehicle will be used for delivery driving.

Delivery platforms must, at their own expense, take out and maintain a personal accident insurance policy to cover employee-like workers.

Previously, not all workers received these protections because they were considered independent contractors.

Under new standards, Australian food delivery drivers will be granted minimum pay and more protections. Credit: The Feed

In 2023, Uber warned the government that reforms to the gig economy would lead to "catastrophic" job losses. That same year, DoorDash also claimed that food delivery prices could more than triple under a worst-case scenario analysis.

Both companies have since walked back these comments and engaged with the TWU on the new standards.

Ed Kitchen, managing director of Uber Eats in Australia and New Zealand, said he is "proud" to have worked on the industry-first framework.

"This is a great moment for gig workers who play such a critical role in Australia's economy and in the lives of millions of Aussies who rely on food delivery every day."

title: 'It's not easy': The hidden pressure point at Australia's airports
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's air traffic control workforce is in the spotlight amid days of flight delays and a near collision at Sydney Airport.

Experts say the job is highly specialised and requires years of experience to ensure public safety is not compromised.

On Tuesday, many Australians arrived at the airport with their plane waiting on the tarmac and clear skies overhead — only to discover their flight had been delayed.

Around 200 flights moving through Melbourne and Perth Airports were forecast to experience delays, according to a daily plan issued by Airservices Australia.

In Sydney, 138 flights were expected to be impacted by ground delays of around 43 minutes, in part due to strong winds, the government-owned air traffic management organisation said.

Rob Sharp, CEO of Airservices Australia, acknowledged that flight delays and disruptions can cause "very high frustration levels" for passengers, airlines and airport partners alike.

Behind the scenes, delays are often used to ensure public safety is not compromised during what Sharp described as a "challenging period" for air traffic controllers.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We do this through effectively putting space between aircraft. But it does come at a cost, and that cost is delays," Sharp said during a press conference on Monday.

His comments follow significant delays to flights on Friday and Saturday last week. On Sunday, two passenger jets also narrowly avoided a ground collision at Sydney Airport, with the incident now under investigation.

It's left industry leaders and aviation experts questioning whether Australia's air traffic control workforce can keep up with aviation demands.

Who's in control?

Uğur Turhan is a senior lecturer in aviation at the University of New South Wales in Canberra. He said controllers are responsible for air traffic safety and efficiency, both on the ground and in the air.

"You cannot put somebody as a high-performing air-traffic controller in one day or one year ... generally, we think that five years' experience is a really good level to perform at high levels in complex traffic situations," Turhan told SBS News.

There are three types of controllers — tower controllers, terminal controllers and en route controllers — responsible for various stages of flights including take-off, landing and airspace movement.

Air traffic controllers are responsible for ensuring safe and efficient aircraft journeys. Source: SBS News / Adobe Stock / Hikari Vector Studio

While training programs vary, typically air traffic controllers train for 12 months before undergoing additional on-the-job training.

Australian air services manage more than 51 million square kilometres of airspace, equivalent to approximately 11 per cent of the world's airspace. This area is managed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, Airservices Australia said.

Federal Transport Minister Catherine King believes the work of air traffic controllers is a "really stressful and difficult job".

READ MORE How do other countries compensate passengers for delayed and cancelled flights?

"If you've been in an air traffic control tower, you've seen the number of flights they are managing, the complexities in how quickly they have to think. It's a really specialised job."

She held emergency meetings in Canberra on Monday following recent flight disruptions. King described her discussion with Sharp from Airservices Australia as "constructive" and said she felt "confident" the organisation was doing "everything they can to get on top of this".

Staff shortages

National disruptions due to air traffic control have fallen by 86 per cent over the past financial year, according to Airservices Australia. Ground delays caused by air services also reduced by 13 per cent.

The air traffic industry has recorded an uptick in staffing, with a record 109 new controllers employed last year. Sharp told the ABC's 7.30 on Monday there were now more than 1,070 air traffic controllers in Australia.

There are an additional 15 people in training, expected to join the workforce by the end of 2027, King said in a press conference on Monday. Experienced air traffic controllers have also been hired from overseas to work in Australia.

Sharp said the sector has traditionally relied on high staff overtime, which he does not believe is a "sustainable model" as Australian airports expand. He said new rostering systems are likely to ease staff burdens from September this year.

Turhan acknowledged the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the aviation industry too.

"Globally, we had COVID-19. We lost some manpower capability in aviation, not just for air traffic controllers. As I said, it is not easy to put someone, with a high performance level in [the job in] just one year; it takes time."

Between October 2021 and December 2022, more than 180 air traffic controllers accepted voluntary redundancies, according to online information published by the Brisbane Flight Path Community Alliance.

COVID-19 had a significant impact on Australia's aviation industry due to travel restrictions and a decline in passenger demand. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

Turhan believes Sydney Airport is a particularly challenging environment for new air traffic controllers. It requires workers to train for two years, plus an additional two years to embed into the system, according to Sharp from Airservices Australia.

"It has a really complex layout ... and also it is operated by different domestic and international terminals," Turhan said.

"In Sydney Airport ... you cannot operate your flights during the night. So, during that limited time you should perform all traffic in a short time and traffic levels are not homogeneously distributed to the time. So, we have peak traffic."

A global issue?

Air traffic control is a highly competitive field which can offer high pay. The base salary for an initial trainee air traffic controller begins at $60,000, which increases to more than $171,000 for a Level 5 controller. Workers at a Level 10 classification can earn over $243,000, and supervisors more than $286,000.

Angus Mitchell, the chief commissioner of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, said it's also considered a specialised profession.

"Airports are incredibly busy. You've got planes taking off, planes landing, planes being manoeuvred across crossing runways, across taxiways. It is a complex environment, but it needs to also be incredibly robust," Mitchell told SBS News.

"Even at low speeds, there can be very significant outcomes if planes come into contact with each other."

This complexity has fuelled a global shortage in air traffic controllers.

In July 2025, United States transportation secretary Sean Duffy told Congress it would cost US$31.5 billion ($44.6 billion) to fully modernise the country's air traffic control system. That same year, the Federal Aviation Administration told US media it was facing a shortage of around 3,000 air traffic controllers.

In July 2026, Singapore announced new air traffic controller recruits would receive a sign-on bonus of SGD$20,000 (approximately $22,100), as Changi Airport is expanded.

Parts of Europe, including Athens Airport in Greece, have experienced flight delays amidst seasonal summer travel peaks.

Air traffic control is used to manage the safe and orderly flow of aircraft into, out of and across international airspace. Source: AP / Carrie Antlfinger

However, Turhan cautioned against comparing Australia's situation directly with Europe.

"In Australia, we have really broad and wide airspace. We have a few big airports but they are busy, and they're handling different kinds of traffic levels."

He is optimistic that discussions about Australia's air traffic control sector could eventually lead to reduced workloads, improved working conditions and fatigue management.

title: November 'circled' as pivotal month for Aussie household budgets
text:
IN BRIEF Nearly half of experts surveyed by Finder expect at least one more rate rise this year, with most tipping November.

Average mortgage borrowers are already paying $359 more a month in interest than they were in January.

While Australian borrowers have avoided another interest rate hike, some economists warn the relief may be short-lived, tipping November as the next key month to watch for a potential rate rise.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision on Tuesday to hold the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent was widely expected, with 92 per cent of experts and economists surveyed by comparison site Finder correctly predicting the outcome.

However, 44 per cent of the panellists still expect at least one more rate rise this year.

Of those expecting an increase, 69 per cent nominated November as the most likely month, prompting Finder to say "November is circled".

KPMG chief economist Brendan Rynne told ABC News the market was anticipating a November hike, giving the RBA more time to assess upcoming economic data.

He said the September-quarter inflation figures and labour market data will give the central bank more information before it makes its next major decision.

"One would expect the rate hike still has to be on the table at some point," he said.

He noted the economy was still running at full capacity, with unemployment at 4.4 per cent and public sector spending continuing to add to demand.

With household spending still relatively strong, Rynne said the RBA may ultimately need to rely on higher interest rates to slow demand and bring inflation back towards its 2 to 3 per cent target range.

Why rates could still rise again

The RBA has already raised interest rates three times this year as it attempts to bring inflation back towards the midpoint of its target range.

"The only way we're going to see a drop in spending in this country is probably from the household sector," Rynne said.

A further rate rise would put additional pressure on households by increasing the cost of borrowing, potentially reducing consumer spending.

Rynne said falling house prices could also affect how Australians spend, through what economists call the "wealth effect".

"As we feel like our house prices are starting to decline, we feel less wealthy and consume less," he said.

But the strength of the labour market means households are still spending, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

"We've never had more Australians employed than we have at the moment," Rynne said.

The 'big four' banks are now predicting a rate hold

The major banks have also shifted their forecasts following lower-than-expected inflation data released last month.

Westpac recently scrapped its prediction of an August rate rise and said it now expects the RBA to leave rates unchanged for the rest of 2026.

ANZ is also forecasting an extended hold at 4.35 per cent, while the Commonwealth Bank expects rates to remain unchanged into 2027.

NAB's forecast similarly points to an extended period at the current rate.

UBS Global Wealth Management's head of Australian equities, Mike Jenneke, told SBS News he was pencilling in one more rate rise in November, although he stressed there was not a high degree of conviction around the call and agreed the tightening cycle was nearing its end.

"The main concern we have is that the RBA has missed its inflation target now for several years and the journey to target remains gradual and is at risk of being derailed," Jenneke said.

A further rate rise would put additional pressure on households by increasing the cost of borrowing. Source: AAP

Meanwhile, Ebury chief economist Anthony Malouf told SBS News he expected the RBA to keep rates on hold until the middle of 2027.

He said he expected the cutting cycle to begin in the second half of next year, with August currently pencilled in for the first cut.

What would another hike mean for borrowers?

Australians with mortgages are already paying substantially more following the rate increases earlier this year.

Finder analysis shows someone with an average home loan of $734,878 is now paying an additional $359 a month in interest compared with January.

That's equivalent to more than $4,300 a year.

Another rate rise could push the average borrower's additional monthly interest payments above $400.

Finder personal finance specialist Taylor Blackburn said Tuesday's hold would give borrowers "another moment to catch their breath", but warned the relief could be short-lived.

"With nearly half of our panel expecting another hike this year, now is the right time to act," Blackburn said.

He urged borrowers who had not reviewed their mortgage or considered refinancing in the past year to check whether they could secure a better deal.

Why November isn't a certainty

While November has been tipped as the most likely month for another increase among those expecting one this year, the RBA is not locked into that path.

The central bank will have more data to consider before its November meeting, including September-quarter inflation and further information about employment and household spending.

Rynne said the board would need to weigh those figures against the cumulative impact of the three rate rises already delivered this year.

Inflation remains above the RBA's target, meaning the central bank faces a difficult balancing act between bringing prices down and putting further pressure on households and the broader economy.

title: Australia is rolling out a new defence against deadly bird flu
text:
In brief Bird flu vaccinations for native species will be rolled out in the coming weeks, the federal government has announced.

The government said it has around $2 million worth of the vaccine, made up of 1,500 vials.

Birds most at risk of contracting the deadly H5 strain of bird flu will be vaccinated in a bid to stop the virus from decimating vulnerable species.

The first vaccines were set to roll out in coming days, Agriculture Minister Julie Collins announced on Tuesday.

Species in captivity will be prioritised for the vaccination based on their vulnerability and risk of catching the virus.

"We've been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading amongst wild birds. But we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response," Collins told reporters in Canberra.

"Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers, particularly of dead birds and mass mortalities around the country from the H5 bird flu, we have been very clear that this will continue to spread across the country."

While wild birds will be vaccinated if possible, the priority will be on birds in captivity.

The federal government says it has secured 1,500 vials of the vaccine, worth about $2 million.

"The doses vary depending in those vials of the size of the bird," Collins said.

"We have sufficient vaccines in terms of undertaking the initial vaccination program, but we've also been very clear we're working with states and territories, and if we need more vaccines, we're able to secure those."

'Not a standalone solution'

Australia's chief veterinary officer Beth Cookson said vaccines would not be the 'silver bullet' to stop the spread of the bird flu.

"It is not a standalone solution. Biosecurity will remain important, the protection of these species," she said.

"We have been working very carefully for the last 18 months as part of our national preparedness to make sure that we have safety and efficacy data available to us."

More than 200 bird flu deaths have been reported, with the majority of cases in South Australia.

While the flu was first detected in migratory birds, it soon spread to native species.

Collins said reporting of the number of bird flu cases would also change due to the spread of the virus among species.

Counting the number of cases was no longer the most accurate picture of how the disease was spreading, the minister said.

"Our reporting will evolve to focus on confirmed H5 events and the developments that matter most, where the disease is spreading, new locations or species affected in emerging areas of risk," she said.

The deadly strain has not been detected in the poultry sector or in the broader agricultural industry to date.

Adelaide University associate professor Mohammed Alsharifi, an influenza vaccination expert, said the rollout of the immunisation would be crucial.

"It's the right approach if we want to keep or conserve those species, because the virus is very lethal and we've seen dead animals around in the news everywhere," he said.

"We need to remember the virus may mutate. But at least if we have good immunity against the clade (variety) of the virus that's circulating, then it will be the right approach."

title: Thousands of hectares burnt as El Niño intensifies Indonesia's dry season
text:
In brief Indonesia is expected to experience a difficult dry season this year, with a high risk of forest fires.

A strong El Niño is one of the drivers, and concerns are growing about what it could mean for Australia's fire outlook.

Dozens of Indonesian schools were shut for a second day on Tuesday as forest fires continued to burn during an intense dry season expected to be worsened by El Niño.

In West Kalimantan on the island of Borneo that Indonesia shares with Malaysia and Brunei, the mayor of the capital Pontianak ordered schools closed due to the smoke wafting over the city from fires elsewhere.

Public records show Pontianak, with a population of around 660,000 people, has tens of thousands of public school pupils.

Children will learn from home for as long as air quality remains poor, mayor Edi Rusdi Kamtono said in a statement, without stating how many schools were affected.

"We have started to feel it, especially at night and in the morning, as haze has already blanketed the city of Pontianak," he said.

On the island of Java, firefighters battled flames for a ninth day at a national park that has lost 900 hectares to an inferno that broke out on Monday last week.

The blaze at the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, a major tourist attraction closed to visitors since Saturday, is one of several fires that have drawn in nearly 50,000 firefighters countrywide.

Indonesia is forecast to experience an unusually tough dry season this year with a high risk for drought and wildfires due in part to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the BMKG weather agency has said.

More than 107,000 hectares of land have burnt countrywide so far this year.

Authorities insist that food stocks remain adequate.

Burnt area in East Java the size of 1,200 football fields

The fire at the Bromo park in East Java has consumed nearly 900 hectares by Tuesday morning.

This is equivalent to over 1,200 football fields and nearly 2 per cent of the total park area.

"We’re making our best effort and mobilising everything ... to extinguish and wet-down the area," local disaster official Satriyo Nurseno said.

"We hope that today we can put out the fire in all areas, then carry out soaking so that the fire does not reignite."

Three water-bombing helicopters and fire trucks were providing support to about 200 firefighters, forest rangers, police and soldiers helping to put out the blaze.

According to the BNPB disaster agency, more than 48,000 personnel have been deployed to fight fires in six provinces.

Security minister Djamari Chaniago said on Monday Indonesia has deployed 43 helicopters and up to 15 fixed-wing planes for cloud seeding where needed.

The process involves spraying particles such as silver iodide and salt from aircraft to produce rainfall, but depends on clouds being present.

As Indonesia braces for the worst effects of El Niño, the BMKG said the average air temperature in July was 27C — higher than the 26.2C average.

It was the highest such jump for July since 1991.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns.

In India and Southeast Asia, it typically causes drier conditions.

The last El Niño helped make 2023 and 2024 the two hottest years globally on record.

The land lost to wildfires in Indonesia so far this year is double the area burnt in 2023.

Concerns for Australia's bushfire season as El Niño intensifies

While an El Niño does not necessarily mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia, it does raise the likelihood.

And with the climate driver shaping up to be one of the strongest on record, experts are worried about what it could mean for Australia's bushfire outlook.

Greg Mullins, the former commissioner of Fire and Rescue NSW, recently told SBS News there was "deep concern in all the fire agencies nationally".

However, Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) forecasters say there are signs that rain could disrupt the summer bushfire threat in some areas.

"That drier than average pattern that we're seeing for September does break down for much of the country and we start seeing either above average rainfall being favoured or even a not-clear signal for a lot of the country," BoM climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua said.

title: Australia v the world: Why our official interest rate stands out
text:
in brief The RBA has kept interest rates on hold at 4.35 per cent in August.

Australia's cash rate target and inflation is higher than some other comparable economies.

Australia's cash rate remains higher than those of several comparable economies after the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) left it unchanged at 4.35 per cent on Tuesday.

The decision underscores a key difference between Australia and many of its peers: inflation has proved more persistent, prompting the central bank to take a more cautious approach to cutting rates.

In its statement of monetary policy, the board explained its widely-anticipated decision was affected by global uncertainty and high inflation in 2026.

"The board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded," it said in its board statement announcing the decision to leave the cash rate on hold.

"While the impact of the Middle East conflict on inflation has so far been less than expected, headline inflation is still too high."

It said trimmed mean inflation — which strips out volatile items — also remained elevated and was "little changed form the March quarter".

Source: SBS News

The latest inflation data showed signs of cooling but it is still running about the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band, and the ongoing global uncertainty is likely to give the central bank "reason to pause", according to AMP chief economist Shane Oliver.

Oliver described interest rates as a "blunt instrument" for central banks around the world to reduce households' spending on discretionary items and tackle inflation.

So how do Australia's interest rates compare globally?

How Australia compares globally

Oliver explained that, historically, levers reserve banks can pull have been the best way to tackle inflation.

Relying on governments alone to help doesn't work as well, he said, because governments can be incentivised to spend more to win votes, even when inflation is high.

Source: SBS News

Cash rate targets differ around the world but share the unifying goal of keeping inflation down and promoting a high-employment economy.

Australia's cash rate target of 4.35 per cent is higher than those of other countries, such as the United States at 3.5-3.75 per cent, the UK at 3.75 per cent, and Canada at 2.25 per cent.

Australia also has higher core inflation, a measure stripping out economic volatility, than these other economies.

Professor and economist Warwick McKibbin from the Australian National University said that trends such as oil supply shocks can impact inflation globally.

Domestic factors, such as economic structure and openness to trade, can also play a part.

Different countries also have different goals for inflation, he said.

"The US has an inflation target of 2 per cent, that's the Federal Reserve's goal," McKibbin said.

"And so, historically, inflation generally doesn't rise significantly above that, although it actually has since COVID-19."

Source: SBS News

Meanwhile, Australia's inflation target is between 2 and 3 per cent, which can also lead to marginally higher inflation.

"What drives actual inflation is both expectations of inflation as well as what's happening in the economy," McKibbin said.

"So you'd expect our inflation rate's probably going to have a higher number than the US because our expectations will be leveraged somewhere between two and three, and that matters as well."

Aside from its inflation target, the RBA's other mandate is to support full employment, meaning as many Australians as possible in work without creating excessive inflation.

While Australia has higher inflation and a higher cash rate target than some other countries, it also has a healthy unemployment rate of 4.4 per cent, lower than the UK, Canada and New Zealand.

What's ahead?

Oliver said that the Australian economy has become more inflation-prone than that of some other countries over the last two years.

"And that is a concern, and something that the Reserve Bank has to be aware of and a reason why they need to be more cautious," he said.

"The RBA will likely retain a tightening bias as it does whatever is necessary to bring inflation down to target."

Australia's 'big four' banks — the Commonwealth Bank, NAB, Westpac and ANZ — don't expect any further movement this year.

But they all anticipate a cut in 2027.

ANZ expects a 0.25 percentage point cut in September and December, lowering the cash rate to 3.85 per cent by the end of 2027

Commonwealth expects cuts in May and August, bringing the rate to 3.85 per cent by the third quarter

NAB forecasts three cuts — in June, September and December — taking the cash rate to 3.60 per cent

Westpac expects cuts in August and December, taking the rate to 3.85 per cent

But Oliver said the RBA wouldn’t hesitate to lift rates in 2026 if needed.

Why some experts still predict another RBA rate rise

The overwhelming majority of economists expect the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to hold the cash rate at 4.35 per cent today, but there are still concerns another rate rise could be needed later this year.

A Finder survey of 38 economists and experts, released on Friday, found 92 per cent expect a hold today.

But the outlook is less certain beyond this meeting, with 44 per cent forecasting at least one more rate rise before the end of 2026.

So, what is behind the more hawkish forecasts?

Andrew Wilson of My Housing Market told Finder underlying inflation remains stubbornly high, with the RBA's preferred measure still well above its 2 to 3 per cent target range.

Source: SBS

He pointed to higher fuel, electricity, rental and construction costs as potential sources of further inflationary pressure.

Queensland University of Technology adjunct professor Noel Whittaker also told Finder the decision was a "line ball call", citing rising fuel and construction costs, uncertainty around the war in the Middle East and reports of continued strong consumer spending.

The concern is that if spending remains resilient while inflation stays above target, the RBA may need to do more to cool demand.

But the case for a hold remains stronger for now.

ANZ's Madeline Dunk told Finder that lower-than-expected trimmed mean inflation and a higher-than-expected unemployment rate give the RBA room to wait and see how the economy evolves.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the latest inflation, labour and housing data should allow the RBA to remain in "wait and see" mode, although he expects the bank to retain a tightening bias while inflation remains too high.

So while today's decision is widely expected to be a hold, the possibility of another hike has not disappeared from the outlook.

title: Car insurance is rising far faster than inflation. What’s driving the jump?
text:
in brief Car insurance premiums are rising far faster than inflation, leaving drivers to shoulder steep increases.

ASIC says customers are not getting enough information from insurers.

Drivers could be paying hundreds of dollars more for car insurance without knowing why their premiums have jumped so sharply, as insurers offer little transparency about the forces driving costs higher.

Car insurance premiums rose 8 per cent in the 12 months to July 2025, more than twice the 3 per cent increase in the broader consumer price index, putting pressure on household budgets even as overall inflation has eased.

While several factors — including higher repair costs, taxes and theft — have contributed to the rise, insurance providers failed to explain to customers why their premiums were going up, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) found in a report released on Tuesday.

"Most insurers gave only generic explanations in supplementary documents, with some providing no explanations at all," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

"This fails to meet the needs of customers trying to understand the reasons for significant price increases."

Without being told the reasons for their premium increase, customers were being denied crucial information needed to decide whether to stay with their current insurer or shop around, Kirkland said.

A spokesperson for Insurance Council of Australia said the industry recognised the need to support customers in understanding what they are paying and why.

"Premiums have been under pressure across the country due to a range of factors including escalating extreme weather costs, insurance-linked taxes, and rising repair and vehicle parts costs, with motor claims costs up 47 per cent since 2020 and building costs up 44 per cent since 2022," the spokesperson said.
