title: Wall Street is about to sell AI bonds. What could go wrong?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessBanking & financeAI Opinion Wall Street is about to sell AI bonds. What could go wrong? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 13, 2026 — 12:16pm

August 13, 2026 — 12:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What do you do when your financial capacity to help your customers buy your products becomes stretched? You turn to Wall Street, of course. That’s what Nvidia has done, enlisting some of the biggest names in private capital – Goldman Sachs, Apollo Global, KKR, Brookfield and Black Rock – to arrange a pool of $US500 billion ($708 billion) or more of capital to help fund purchases of Nvidia chips. Nvidia needs money - and Wall Street is keen to provide it. Bloomberg The firms haven’t actually committed that much capital – they’ve signed memorandums of understanding, not lines of credit – and every project brought before them will be individually evaluated. Nevertheless, Wall Street has provided a signal of intent.

Advertisement

With Nvidia’s own ability to continue to effectively provide vendor financing for purchases of its chips – the “circular financing” arrangements that have been increasingly scrutinised and criticised – perhaps constrained, it wants to enlarge that circle – and it’s Wall Street’s access to vast pools of private capital that will enable that. Not that Nvidia won’t contribute. It says it will guarantee 25 per cent of the residual value of the collateral for any project. For the Wall Street firms, the allure is that it could create a new class of asset-backed securities that they can on-sell to pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and wealthy investors, clipping the tickets on the way through. The company refers to those projects – the chips and data centres and other infrastructure that support the training of AI models – as “AI factories,” but two-thirds or more of the value of those factories will lie in the value of its own chips. That’s potentially a $US125 billion exposure for Nvidia, its shareholders and creditors. For Nvidia, the concept is designed to increase the capacity of its non-hyperscaler customers to fund the purchases of its chips.

Advertisement

Sharemarkets and conventional lenders have become warier, and more discerning, about the AI companies they are prepared to back now that the hyperscalers are out-spending their cashflows and competing for equity and debt. The cost of equity and debt for the smaller entities is becoming prohibitive. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The AI spending frenzy is giving investors anxiety Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist For the Wall Street firms, the allure of the concept is that it could create a new class of asset-backed securities that they can on-sell to pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and wealthy investors, clipping the tickets, naturally, on the way through. The “AI factories,” are, however, rather different to the asset classes that are usually securitised. The cash flows from securitised residential and commercial mortgages, or infrastructure assets, or corporate loans are high quality and supported by cashflows and collateral that tend to increase in value over time.

Advertisement

The core assets of the AI factories, the Nvidia chips, have more limited and uncertain lifespans. The income streams they might generate and their value as collateral is less certain, but almost certainly diminishes over time. There’s a debate about the useful lives of chips, given that Nvidia (and others) produces a “next generation” chip with superior capabilities every two years or so. Some argue that their value should be fully depreciated over only three to five years. Nvidia says their useful life can be up to a decade. There’s no doubt, however, that an outdated chip whose use is now to apply the knowledge gained from the training of AI models is less valuable than the latest generation chips being used to train those models. The decline in value over time – and the time period is unknowable today – would erode the value of the collateral, with Nvidia’s guarantee providing the backstop for investors.

Advertisement

What Nvidia and its Wall Street are depicting is a form of collateralised debt, with Nvidia holding the “first loss” tranche that will be called on if a loan defaults and the rate of chip obsolescence is greater than anticipated. With Nvidia’s own ability to provide vendor financing for purchases of its chips constrained, it wants to access Wall Street’s vast pools of private capital. Bloomberg Wall Street is good at financial engineering a solution to difficult financial challenges and, faced with funding the biggest investment boom in history, there’s no bigger challenge than supplying the capital to acquire the chips and infrastructure for artificial intelligence. It’s not just the scale of the demand for capital – the hyperscalers ( Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) alone are investing about $US750 billion, largely in AI, this year and will spend more than $US1 trillion next year -- but the reality is that AI revenue growth is being far outstripped by the growth rate of the spending. It appears near certain that those hyperscalers, despite their vast legacy cashflows, will all be cash-negative, and more highly leveraged, next year.

Advertisement

Google has raised new equity and most of the big tech companies pursuing AI leadership ambitions have, perhaps for the first time, begun tapping debt markets, with about $US350 billion of AI-related bond issues so far this year. Despite the cash from their non-AI businesses, the spreads on those bonds have been blowing out. Wall Street firms can be ingenious but, as the global financial crisis demonstrated, they sometimes push the risk envelope too far. Independent AI promoters like OpenAI and Anthropic have raised their capital from private investors and are, like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, planning initial public offerings to access the bigger pool of equity capital in the listed market. Any debt they have raised – and SpaceX has raised debt – would be priced as “junk” and be costly. At those companies’ rates of investment, however – and the market’s satiation with all things AI – the planned listings might provide a bandaid, not a cure, for their financial stress. At face value, gaining access to the estimated $US22 trillion of private capital could provide the extra funding required, and provide it on more attractive/less expensive terms than are currently available to individual AI borrowers.

Advertisement

Securitising debts – packaging up parcels of loans and therefore diversifying the risks – would create securities with much stronger credit quality than that of an individual AI borrower. As was discovered in 2008 and the sub-prime mortgage crisis, however, bundling poor credits together doesn’t necessarily alter the reality that they are risky loans that could all go south together. Related Article Opinion

AI Scared by tech’s debt deluge, investors are questioning the AI boom Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist As the Nvidia chips age, the value of the collateral that the end-investors holding those bundles rely on would be diminishing. And even that diminished value would be vulnerable as inference chips become increasingly commoditised. That’s the segment of the sector – the applications of AI – that China is strategically targeting, with chips whose prices already significantly undercut their US counterparts. The collateral, in the event of a default, could be near-worthless.

Advertisement

The Wall Street firms are no doubt comforted by Nvidia’s guarantee, but the tech giant is at the epicentre of the boom in AI and AI valuations and has – due to its myriad of circular financing deals in a sector where there are now layers of circularity to financial relationships – a leveraged exposure to the fate of that boom. The degree of financial engineering already pervasive in the sector and the extent to which the off-balance-sheet liabilities of AI’s blue-chip companies, estimated at more than $US1.6 trillion, now surpass their debt on the balance sheet, say that all the conventional funding options for AI in the US have been stretched to their limits. In a sense, the agreement Nvidia unveiled with the Wall Street players underscores how fragile the AI ecosystem now is. Unable to raise sufficient funds conventionally, the sector is being forced to turn to a bespoke, unconventional, financially engineered structure to try to sustain its insatiable appetite for risk capital. Wall Street firms can be ingenious but, as the global financial crisis demonstrated, they sometimes push the risk envelope too far, with unpleasant consequences.

title: I signed up for the outback’s Squid Game. Now I look like a gaudy octopus
text:

LifestyleLife & relationshipsThe Kimberley Opinion I signed up for the outback’s Squid Game. Now I look like a gaudy octopus Far from the comforts of home, I found something more consoling. Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age August 13, 2026 — 11:53am

August 13, 2026 — 11:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A veteran of the country’s north-west once told me, “You come out of the Kimberley to recover.” He was right. Everything in that gargantuan rockery is anathema to a modern human’s comfort, the place is a Thoreauvian sequence of Squid Game. I have so many welts, bites, stings, abrasions and bruises covering me that I look like a trespasser brought down by birdshot before being flogged. The pharmaceuticals are useless; swellings flicker and flare floridly across my hide like the bioluminescence on certain gaudy octopus that pulse and shimmer when goaded by a shark or an Attenborough. To walk the wild Kimberley is to make innumerable staccato decisions – where to step, which piece of stone might tip you headfirst into a sandstone crevasse garnished with spinifex? Which route will lead into a tangle of vine and elephant grass? Which into head-high spinifex and a barrage of eager green ants? Even camel hate spinifex, each plant a supernova of spines containing toxins to inflame, blister and infect your skin. Photo: Robin Cowcher Every day at walk’s end I used a hunting knife to lever ticks from my crevices as if I were a carpenter prising roofing nails from tin ... and then whisky to aid sleep on rock, of course, always rock, amid the screech and wing beat of bats as big as corgis. We were as remote as any place on today’s planet. On a plateau overlooking a wild river we found a cave mouth shaped like a gaping wound in a rock face three metres above the ground. Climbing to it, we found inside a conch shell the size of a football. Its patterns had faded to white.

Advertisement

How many years had it been here, carried two days’ walk from the sea – 200? 20,000? Had it been traded? How had it been got from the water among the massive crocodiles at this river’s mouth? Shells are as beautiful as flowers, but rarer and less ephemeral. This one must have been a treasure to its owners, likely handed from one keeper to the next through generations. Related Article Opinion

Celebrity life There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age The cave looked down on an amphitheatre of orange stone, its pillars and protrusions decorated with ceremonial figures the colour of dried blood. They were leaping and dancing, dressed in feathered skirts, elbow and knee bands and massive feathered headdresses like stooks of hay. It was as fine a place for ceremony as anything wrought by Christopher Wren. As I turned the huge shell in my hands it occurred to me that it was a musical instrument, as sonically profound and elemental to an ancient liturgy as a church organ, sitting there in the wall. And I suppose the figures dancing on the stone were dancing to notes once blown from this exotic instrument by some excited musician, some hopeful composer smiling as he brought the thing to his lips, some Amadeus delighted to watch the folk lose themselves in his notes, happily leading them on to abandon. The amphitheatre came alive for me and I could see the leaping shadows flickering in the firelight on the stone walls and hear the many singers, their voices echoing off the rock back into the dance in a feedback loop that must have sounded like affirmation from the pertinent spirits, freeing the whole on to higher enchantment.

Advertisement

Parents hefted toddlers aloft in the dance, larger children mimicked the moves of the cooler adults, old folk sat at the dance’s edge not wanting to dull the exuberance with their limited footwork, but smiling, approving, occasionally shouting encouragement. I imagined the whole corroboree as a kind of ecstatic gospel service in one of those churches in the US South that birth famous musicians, famous music and unparallelled emotion. All of it enabled by this conch shell I held in my hands, this invaluable gastropod trumpet blown by a barefoot Dizzy Gillespie. Ancient Aboriginal art in the Kimberley. I hefted the conch and lifted it towards my mouth, thinking I might attempt some antique note, some brief replication of a sound the blood dark figures on the walls might recognise and come alive to. But I didn’t do it. Nor would I pull the stops on a pipe organ in a deconsecrated church. We climbed up and put the conch back in the cave on the stone where we found it. It sits there in a place once central, sacred, now remote, an inanimate thing suffused with ghostly history and wondrous potential, like a church organ awaiting an organist and congregation that will never come again. title: Chaos at Sydney airport as passengers grounded
text:
Thousands of more passengers at Sydney Airport are facing frustrating waits as the chaotic scenes which saw more than 100 delays on Friday continues.

For the second day in a row, the number of flights delayed hit triple figures, with 150 services impacted.

The disruption saw at least 110 international and domestic flights postponed, with some aircraft left sitting on the tarmac for two hours.

And while Airservice Australia said the issues on Friday had been resolved, the organisation confirmed on Saturday that "roster restraints" continued to affect the airport.

Stephen Beckett, chief executive of industry group Airlines for Australia and New Zealand, said thousands of passengers were affected.

"We understand that they are again struggling to have enough people rostered on in the air traffic control tower to keep air services operating efficiently," he said.

"The advice we've received is that both international and domestic flights are impacted. We have more than 150 delays this morning."

Qantas, Australia's largest airline, is reported to be heavily impacted, with 95 delays across its network.

As of Saturday morning, several services continued to experience disruption, including an international arrival from Kuala Lumpur which is set to land close to four hours late.

Domestic arrivals from Brisbane, Melbourne and Canberra are also not set to land on schedule, while a service from Wagga Wagga is expected to be almost two hours late.

A spokesman for Airservices Australia said on Saturday that roster constraints continued to be affecting the airport.

"Airservices Australia has enacted Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) measures including departure spacing at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport today due to roster constraints, to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands," a statement read.

"Airservices acknowledges the ATFM measures may cause some disruptions to airline scheduling and is working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible.

"Airservices is enhancing our training pipeline to add further controllers to improve roster depth and is working to address rostering issues that reduce the flexibility of our workforce."

The Sydney Airport website also crashed shortly after 2pm: "There might be too much traffic or a configuration error", the website error message said.

In a statement, Airservices Australia said it had delayed the flights because of "operational restrictions".

The government-owned corporation "enacted Air Traffic Flow Management measure at Sydney Airport", "due to operational restrictions to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands".

"Airservices acknowledges the (air traffic flow management) measures, which have now been removed, caused disruptions to airline scheduling, however capacity has now been restored and no further significant delays are anticipated," the spokesman said.

title: ICAC accused keen to ‘exonerate’ himself

The long-time chief executive of NSW's peak body for Catholic schools is keen to exonerate himself at an explosive anti-corruption inquiry that has ensnared the highest echelons of the state Liberal Party, a hearing has been told.

title: Disconnected: reform urged as rural Aussies left behind
text:
Telcos and the industry watchdog are calling for major reform as rural Australians experience poor connectivity and sometimes rely on century-old technology to communicate.

Mobile and internet connectivity in the bush remains unreliable and outages risk lives and economies, according to an analysis of more than 25,000 complaints to the watchdog.

The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman's report Left Behind, released on Thursday, recommended a review of complex regulatory frameworks that govern the sector.

It also recommended consumer compensation options, remedies to poor mobile connectivity and digital literacy campaigns.

Mobile connection in the bush remains patchy and a risk to lives, the ombudsman found. (Stephanie Gardiner/AAP PHOTOS)

"Reliable telecommunications aren't a luxury," ombudsman Cynthia Gebert told AAP.

"They're essential for safety, for economic participation in everyday life."

The 2024 shut-down of the ageing 3G network left some rural communities without any mobile coverage, as farmers described having to either travel to make calls or rely on two-way radios.

"It's fine, but everyone in the district can hear what you're saying, so you have to juggle what you say," one rural resident told the ombudsman.

Advertisement Advertisement

Another described a lack of connectivity more frankly: "No doubt it's because we're in the middle of nowhere. Who gives a shit about us, right?"

A rural firefighter reported triple-zero dropping out while he responded to a fatal blaze and being unable to call a colleague standing 100m away.

The ombudsman found telcos are not responding to the challenges facing rural consumers. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

The report also found consumers living in remote areas had difficulty accessing upgrades and repairs, with one man making several 350km trips just to set-up a new device.

The telecommunication sector's peak body said it welcomed calls to cut red tape so it could accelerate the roll-out of 5G, fibre and satellite technology.
